The apparent arc followed by the Sun across the sky during a day. Its height, direction and duration above the horizon depend on latitude and date. Comparing paths explains seasonal changes in daylight and in the length of shadows.

The angular position of the Sun north or south of the celestial equator, equivalent to the latitude of the subsolar point. It varies between about 23.44° north and south through the year and helps determine noon altitude and daylight duration.

The Sun’s angle above the horizon at local solar noon. In a simple geometric calculation it is 90° minus the absolute difference between latitude and solar declination. A negative value means the Sun remains below the horizon at noon.

The time between sunrise and sunset at a place. It varies mainly with latitude and the time of year because Earth has a tilted axis. Day length differs from the approximately 24-hour solar day, which includes darkness.
The part of a sundial that casts a shadow. For a vertical gnomon on level ground, shadow length depends on its height and the Sun's altitude.

The region between the Tropic of Cancer and Tropic of Capricorn, approximately 23.44 degrees north and south. The Sun can be directly overhead only within this belt, on dates determined by latitude. Tropical climates still vary greatly in rainfall and elevation.

The angular position of a place north or south of the equator, expressed in degrees. Latitude helps determine solar altitude and seasonal day length. Lines of equal latitude are parallels, unlike meridians, which measure longitude.

misconception.claim: The Sun is directly overhead at local noon everywhere on Earth.
misconception.truth: Local solar noon is when the Sun reaches its daily highest position, but that position need not be overhead. Noon altitude depends on latitude and solar declination. The Sun can be directly overhead only between the tropics, and only on dates appropriate to the latitude.

misconceptions.claim: The Sun is directly overhead at local noon everywhere on Earth.
misconceptions.truth: Local solar noon is when the Sun reaches its daily highest position, but that position need not be overhead. Noon altitude depends on latitude and solar declination. The Sun can be directly overhead only between the tropics, and only on dates appropriate to the latitude.

teacher.script:
Locate the horizon, solar path and selected Sun position. Move Local solar time from morning to afternoon and follow the Sun across the sky.

Change Latitude and Date, then compare the highest solar altitude and length of daylight. Look for a date and latitude with no sunset.
pitfalls: Use geographic north and south when describing the Sun’s path; a magnetic compass may require a local correction.
Explain that an overhead noon Sun is possible only within the tropics.
Compare both noon solar altitude and daylight duration when changing the latitude or season.

modelNotes: If you cannot move latitude in your head from 51.5° to 0°, you cannot compare a UK playground with Nairobi, and you will keep saying the Sun is overhead everywhere at lunch.
Noon altitude is 90° minus the absolute difference of latitude and declination: 90° − |φ − δ|.
Toward the equator: noon stays high, day length sits near 12 h.
Drag Latitude toward 0° for Nairobi, or toward Miami’s band, or south.

labs.title: Continental drift
labs.hook: Continents move with tectonic plates.
labs.objective: Compare reconstructed continental positions through time and use fossil and coastline evidence to discuss the former arrangement of Pangaea.

steps.title: Observe
steps.body: Begin with the older reconstruction and identify the major continental blocks. Compare their positions with the present-day globe.

steps.title: Tinker
steps.body: Move Time before present towards zero and follow India northward. Use geological evidence as well as coastlines when explaining how earlier positions are reconstructed.

steps.title: Explain
steps.body: Which evidence would you use to test the continental arrangement shown in an older reconstruction?

steps.title: Check
steps.body: Choose an answer and explain your reasoning. Each question includes feedback.

choices: A late Palaeozoic–Mesozoic supercontinent, not the only one
questions.explain: Pangaea was assembled by plate convergence long after Earth formed, and other supercontinents existed before it. Its later breakup produced the arrangement from which today's continents developed.

questions.prompt: Wegener’s fit argument is strongest when…
choices: You fit continental shelves, not today’s beaches
questions.explain: Modern shorelines shift with sea level, erosion and sediment deposition. The submerged continental margins therefore provide a better guide to matching former continental edges.
Continents are embedded in lithospheric plates that can also include oceanic crust. Their movement is part of plate motion rather than continents independently pushing through stationary ocean floor.

choices: Continent–continent collision after India walked north
questions.explain: India moved north as part of its plate and eventually collided with Eurasia. Continued convergence shortened and thickened the crust, building the Himalayan mountain belt.

why: Continents move with tectonic plates. Matching geological evidence across oceans helped establish continental drift, and plate reconstructions combine evidence to estimate earlier continental positions.
Move Time before present towards zero and follow India northward. Use geological evidence as well as coastlines when explaining how earlier positions are reconstructed.
Modern coastlines are moved by a reconstruction model; ancient coastlines also depended on sea level, erosion and sedimentation.

glossary.def: A supercontinent assembled during the late Palaeozoic and broken apart during the Mesozoic. Its reconstruction uses evidence from rocks, fossils, magnetism and continental margins. Pangaea was one of several supercontinents in Earth’s history, rather than Earth’s original crust.
The gently sloping, submerged outer part of a continent, extending from the coast to the shelf break.

Earth’s rigid outer mechanical layer, comprising the crust and the uppermost mantle. It is divided into tectonic plates and overlies the weaker asthenosphere. The lithosphere is therefore thicker than the crust alone.

The movement of continents over geological time, proposed by Alfred Wegener using evidence such as matching fossils and rock belts. Plate tectonics later supplied a wider explanation: continents move as parts of lithospheric plates that also include ocean floor.

The formation and outward movement of oceanic crust at a spreading ridge. Magma cools to form new crust as the plates separate. Increasing rock ages and broadly matching magnetic polarity sequences on either side provide evidence for this process.
The descent of one lithospheric plate beneath another into the mantle at a convergent boundary, commonly involving oceanic lithosphere.

A large assembly containing most of Earth’s continental landmasses. Geological evidence records several episodes of assembly and breakup, including Pangaea. Their histories involve different oceans, plate boundaries and timescales rather than a perfectly repeating arrangement.
Comparison of continental margins, rather than modern coastlines, when reconstructing former continental positions. Sediment cover and deformation make the fit approximate.

misconception.claim: Matching modern coastlines is enough to prove how the continents once fitted together.
misconception.truth: Coastlines change with sea level, erosion and deposition, so their fit is approximate. Reconstructions also use continental margins, matching rock sequences and structures, fossils, and magnetic evidence. Agreement among different kinds of evidence provides a stronger basis for estimating past continental positions.

misconceptions.claim: Matching modern coastlines is enough to prove how the continents once fitted together.
misconceptions.truth: Coastlines change with sea level, erosion and deposition, so their fit is approximate. Reconstructions also use continental margins, matching rock sequences and structures, fossils, and magnetic evidence. Agreement among different kinds of evidence provides a stronger basis for estimating past continental positions.

teacher.script:
Begin with the older reconstruction and identify the major continental blocks. Compare their positions with the present-day globe.

Move Time before present towards zero and follow India northward. Use geological evidence as well as coastlines when explaining how earlier positions are reconstructed.
pitfalls: Explain that Pangaea was one of several supercontinents and that oceanic crust moves with the plates.
Use continental margins and geological evidence rather than matching modern beaches alone.
Distinguish a tectonic plate from a country; the United Kingdom moves with the Eurasian plate.

modelNotes: News maps that freeze today’s beaches as eternal outlines hide 250 million years of passengers.
From about 300 to 180 Ma a supercontinent, Pangaea, sat assembled.
The globe uses EarthByte’s Müller 2019 plate reconstruction at 10 Ma intervals.
Set Ma before present to 250 Ma, then compare the 10 Ma snapshots towards the present.
At about 250 Ma the continental shelves fit as Pangaea.

labs.title: Hotspots
labs.hook: A moving plate can carry older volcanoes away from a long-lived region of melting.
labs.objective: Use the direction of increasing volcanic age to infer relative plate motion in the Hawaiian and Yellowstone examples.

steps.title: Observe
steps.body: Locate the young and older ends of the Hawaiian comparison.

steps.title: Tinker
steps.body: Enable Yellowstone and compare its different geographic age direction.

steps.title: Explain
steps.body: How does the direction of increasing volcanic age indicate the plate’s motion relative to the melting region?

steps.title: Check
steps.body: Choose an answer and explain your reasoning. Each question includes feedback.

questions.prompt: Older volcanoes in the main Hawaiian chain generally lie…
choices: Northwest of the currently active southeastern end.
questions.explain: The Pacific Plate carries older Hawaiian volcanoes northwest relative to the active melting region. Newer volcanic centres form near the southeastern end of the chain.

questions.prompt: Older centres in the Yellowstone track lie…
choices: Southwest along the Snake River Plain.
At the same location as every modern eruption.
questions.explain: Volcanic centres become progressively older southwest of Yellowstone along the Snake River Plain. This pattern records motion of the North American Plate relative to the underlying magmatic system.

questions.prompt: A mantle plume is best described here as…
choices: Upwelling hot, mostly solid mantle, with partial melting possible during ascent.
A crack through the inner core.
One shared pipe beneath Hawaiʻi and Yellowstone.
questions.explain: Mantle rock can rise slowly while remaining mostly solid. As pressure falls during ascent, some of that hot rock may cross its melting threshold and generate magma.

why: A moving plate can carry older volcanoes away from a long-lived region of melting. Comparing the direction of increasing age along a volcanic track helps explain relative plate motion.
Enable Yellowstone and compare its different geographic age direction.
The sections illustrate motion and age direction; they do not calculate eruption dates or reproduce the full structure of a mantle plume.

glossary.def: A region of persistent volcanism that can occur within a plate or at a boundary. Many hotspots are associated with mantle upwelling; not all have an established deep plume origin.
An underwater mountain, usually volcanic. Seamounts need not lie on an age-progressive hotspot chain or have once stood above sea level.
An upwelling of unusually hot mantle material that may supply hotspot volcanism. It is mostly deforming solid rock, with partial melting possible near the top.
A large volcanic depression formed mainly when the ground collapses into an underlying magma reservoir after magma is withdrawn.
Volcanoes that get older away from the active centre, recording plate motion.

Volcanic activity occurring within a tectonic plate rather than along its boundary. Hawaiʻi is one example. Possible causes include mantle upwelling and lithospheric processes; its location alone does not establish the depth or structure of the magma source.

Melting of only part of a rock, because its constituent minerals do not all melt under the same conditions. Melt may separate and rise while solid material remains. This helps explain why magma differs in composition from its source rock.
A submerged seamount with a relatively flat summit, commonly formed when a volcanic island is eroded near sea level and later subsides.

misconception.claim: A hotspot must remain perfectly fixed while its plate moves.
misconception.truth: A volcanic age track records motion of a plate relative to a region of melting. Plate motion is important, but the source can also shift as the mantle moves. Track direction and age therefore constrain relative motion without requiring an exactly stationary source.

misconceptions.claim: A hotspot must remain perfectly fixed while its plate moves.
misconceptions.truth: A volcanic age track records motion of a plate relative to a region of melting. Plate motion is important, but the source can also shift as the mantle moves. Track direction and age therefore constrain relative motion without requiring an exactly stationary source.

teacher.script:
Locate the young and older ends of the Hawaiian comparison.

Enable Yellowstone and compare its different geographic age direction.
pitfalls: Treat the selected hotspot examples as separate volcanic systems rather than one continuous plume.
Describe the warm mantle region as mostly solid material that can produce partial melting.
Use the illustrated landforms to explain the process without assigning dates or surveyed dimensions to intermediate frames.

sources.label: USGS: hot but not molten plume material

modelNotes: In the main Hawaiian island chain, older volcanoes generally lie northwest of the currently active southeastern end; Kauaʻi preserves rocks about 5–5.5 Ma old.
The Yellowstone track becomes older southwestwards along the Snake River Plain and extends back roughly 17 Ma.

labs.title: Seafloor spreading
labs.hook: New oceanic crust forms at a spreading ridge and moves away on both sides.
labs.objective: Explain how new oceanic crust forms at a ridge and how magnetic stripes record spreading on either side.

steps.title: Observe
steps.body: Find the ridge axis and the two same-age endpoint labels. Set the full rate to 25 mm/year; calculate the 12.5 mm/year half rate.

steps.title: Tinker
steps.body: Play the magnetic reversal sequence and follow paired markers. Compare wider and narrower stripes without assuming a constant reversal period.

steps.title: Explain
steps.body: Why do matching magnetic stripes appear on opposite sides of a ridge, and what can their widths tell us?

steps.title: Check
steps.body: Choose an answer and explain your reasoning. Each question includes feedback.

questions.explain: Magma rises and solidifies at a spreading ridge, forming new oceanic crust. Continued spreading moves that crust away from the axis, so it generally becomes older with distance.

choices: Both sides of the ridge add crust
questions.explain: New crust forms on both sides of the ridge and records the same sequence of magnetic polarity changes. Spreading carries those records outward into broadly matching bands, although their widths can differ if spreading is asymmetric.

choices: Geomagnetic reversals frozen in cooling basalt
questions.explain: As basalt cools, magnetic minerals lock in a record of the prevailing geomagnetic field. Successive reversals and continued spreading create bands of normal and reversed polarity.

questions.prompt: Old ocean floor is destroyed at…
choices: Trenches such as Cascadia, not at San Andreas
questions.explain: At a subduction trench, oceanic lithosphere bends and descends into the mantle. Transform boundaries mainly accommodate sideways motion and do not perform that recycling process.

why: New oceanic crust forms at a spreading ridge and moves away on both sides. Its age generally increases with distance, while magnetic stripes record changes in Earth’s magnetic polarity.
Play the magnetic reversal sequence and follow paired markers. Compare wider and narrower stripes without assuming a constant reversal period.
The experiment uses a selected spreading history; real ridges change speed and can spread asymmetrically.

glossary.def: The speed at which plates separate at a spreading ridge, usually expressed in centimetres per year. A full spreading rate measures separation across both sides; a half rate measures one side’s motion relative to the ridge, so the convention matters.

A change in the polarity of Earth’s magnetic field. Magnetic minerals in cooling volcanic rock can preserve the field’s direction at the time they formed. Reversals occur at irregular intervals, so magnetic bands do not all represent equal durations.
A submarine mountain system at a spreading boundary, where mantle upwelling and melting form new oceanic crust. Seafloor generally becomes older away from the spreading axis.

The hypothesis linking symmetrical seafloor magnetic anomalies to spreading at ocean ridges and reversals of Earth’s magnetic field. Newly cooled crust records the field at formation. Comparing anomaly sequences with reversal ages provides evidence for plate movement.

The outer rocky layer beneath most ocean basins, composed mainly of basalt and gabbro and averaging about seven kilometres thick. It forms at spreading ridges and is eventually recycled at subduction zones. It is only part of an oceanic plate.

A band of oceanic crust whose magnetic minerals record a particular field polarity. Seafloor spreading carries newly formed crust away from a ridge, producing broadly matching polarity sequences on its two sides. Stripe widths also depend on spreading rate.
The temperature above which a material loses its spontaneous ferromagnetic or ferrimagnetic ordering; about 580 °C for pure magnetite.
A long seafloor feature extending beyond a ridge-offset transform fault. Beyond the active transform segment, both sides move with the same plate.

misconception.claim: Every magnetic stripe on the ocean floor represents the same amount of time.
misconception.truth: Geomagnetic reversals occur at irregular intervals, and spreading rates can change. A stripe’s width depends on both the duration of its polarity interval and the rate at which crust moved away from the ridge. Matching sequences are stronger evidence than an assumption of equally spaced reversals.

misconceptions.claim: Every magnetic stripe on the ocean floor represents the same amount of time.
misconceptions.truth: Geomagnetic reversals occur at irregular intervals, and spreading rates can change. A stripe’s width depends on both the duration of its polarity interval and the rate at which crust moved away from the ridge. Matching sequences are stronger evidence than an assumption of equally spaced reversals.

teacher.script:
Find the ridge axis and the two same-age endpoint labels. Set the full rate to 25 mm/year; calculate the 12.5 mm/year half rate.

Play the magnetic reversal sequence and follow paired markers. Compare wider and narrower stripes without assuming a constant reversal period.
pitfalls: Explain magnetic stripes as records preserved in cooling crust, rather than as waves moving across the seabed.
Compare the age of crust on either side of the ridge, and distinguish spreading from movement along the San Andreas transform system.
Account for the model’s twelvefold vertical exaggeration when interpreting the shape of the ridge.

modelNotes: A full spreading rate of 25 mm/year means each flank moves 12.5 mm/year, or 12.5 km per million years.
Change Full spreading rate and compare ages at the two 50 km endpoints.

labs.title: Atmosphere as a thin film
labs.hook: Atmospheric layers are distinguished mainly by how temperature changes with altitude.
labs.objective: Identify the main atmospheric layers and explain how changes in temperature with height help distinguish them.

steps.title: Observe
steps.body: Open Layer globe and name regions 1–4 using the key. Use Explode to separate the regions, then restore spacing. Switch to physical scale and compare the thickness of the atmosphere with Earth’s radius.

steps.title: Tinker
steps.body: Open Temperature profile. At lapse rate 6.5 °C/km, calculate 15 − 12 × 6.5 = −63 °C. Change the lapse rate to 4 °C/km and compare −33 °C.

steps.title: Explain
steps.body: How does the temperature profile distinguish atmospheric layers that have no solid boundary between them?

steps.title: Check
steps.body: Choose an answer and explain your reasoning. Each question includes feedback.

questions.prompt: Where does almost all weather happen?
questions.explain: The troposphere contains most atmospheric water vapour and supports strong vertical mixing. These conditions concentrate clouds, precipitation and most familiar weather in the lowest atmospheric layer.

choices: Temperature falls about 6.5 °C each kilometre up in the troposphere, on average.
questions.explain: A lapse rate of 6.5 °C/km means the reference temperature decreases by about 6.5 °C for each kilometre of height. Actual atmospheric profiles vary with weather, location and season.

questions.prompt: Why is the stratosphere warmer as you go up?
choices: Closer to the Sun in kilometres that matter.
Ozone absorbs ultraviolet and heats that layer.
It is closer to space heaters.
questions.explain: Ozone absorbs ultraviolet radiation and converts part of that energy into heat. This absorption produces the characteristic temperature increase with height through much of the stratosphere.

questions.prompt: Denver is a mile high. Is its weather still troposphere weather?
choices: No — it is already in space.
Yes. The tropopause is still many kilometres above the city.
No, because air is 100% oxygen there.
questions.explain: Denver's elevation of about 1.6 km is still far below the local tropopause under typical conditions. Its weather therefore occurs within the troposphere despite the city's high elevation.

why: Atmospheric layers are distinguished mainly by how temperature changes with altitude. Most weather occurs in the troposphere, while absorption of ultraviolet radiation helps warm the stratosphere above it.
Open Temperature profile. At lapse rate 6.5 °C/km, calculate 15 − 12 × 6.5 = −63 °C. Change the lapse rate to 4 °C/km and compare −33 °C.
Layer boundaries vary with place and season; the atmosphere is drawn thicker so its vertical structure can be inspected.

glossary.def: The lowest atmospheric layer, containing most air mass and nearly all weather. It is typically about 8 km deep near the poles and 16–18 km near the tropics.
The boundary between the troposphere and stratosphere, identified mainly by a change in the vertical temperature gradient. Its altitude varies with latitude and weather.

The rate at which temperature changes with height in the atmosphere. An environmental lapse rate describes measured surrounding air; an adiabatic rate describes a rising or sinking parcel. An inversion occurs where temperature increases with height.

The atmospheric layer above the troposphere, extending roughly to 50 km altitude. Temperature generally increases with height because ozone absorbs ultraviolet radiation. This stable layering limits the vertical mixing typical of the lower weather layer.
The atmospheric layer roughly 50–85 km above the surface, in which temperature generally falls with altitude. Many meteors become luminous here.
The very thin atmospheric layer above roughly 85 km where kinetic temperature generally rises with altitude as gases absorb energetic solar radiation. Much auroral activity occurs here.

An instrument package carried by a balloon that measures atmospheric properties such as temperature, humidity and pressure as it rises. Tracking its position also reveals winds. A sounding is a vertical sample at a time and place, not a complete atmospheric map.

A region of the stratosphere with a relatively high concentration of ozone. Absorption of ultraviolet radiation helps warm this layer and reduces the amount reaching the ground. It is a diffuse region of gas, rather than a solid protective shell.

misconception.claim: The tropopause is the top of the atmosphere.
misconception.truth: The tropopause marks the boundary between the troposphere and stratosphere. Air continues far above it, becoming progressively less dense. Atmospheric layers are defined mainly by temperature structure, while the tropopause’s height changes with latitude, season and weather.

misconceptions.claim: The tropopause is the top of the atmosphere.
misconceptions.truth: The tropopause marks the boundary between the troposphere and stratosphere. Air continues far above it, becoming progressively less dense. Atmospheric layers are defined mainly by temperature structure, while the tropopause’s height changes with latitude, season and weather.

teacher.script:
Open Layer globe and name regions 1–4 using the key. Use Explode to separate the regions, then restore spacing. Switch to physical scale and compare the thickness of the atmosphere with Earth’s radius.

Open Temperature profile. At lapse rate 6.5 °C/km, calculate 15 − 12 × 6.5 = −63 °C. Change the lapse rate to 4 °C/km and compare −33 °C.
pitfalls: Return exploded layers to their original positions before comparing atmospheric thicknesses.
Explain that the tropopause separates layers within the atmosphere; air continues above it.
Connect stratospheric warming with the absorption of ultraviolet radiation rather than proximity to the Sun.

modelNotes: The reference globe uses boundaries at 12, 50 and 85 km, and shows the thermosphere only as far as 500 km; real boundaries vary.
The troposphere is commonly about 8 km deep near the poles and 16–18 km in the tropics.
At 6.5 °C/km, a 15 °C surface gives −63 °C at 12 km.
If 3D is unavailable, use the ISS limb photograph, definitions and the teacher note.

labs.title: Earth’s energy budget
labs.hook: Earth reflects some incoming sunlight and absorbs the rest.
labs.objective: Trace energy entering and leaving Earth, and explain how reflection and atmospheric absorption affect the surface temperature.

steps.title: Observe
steps.body: Explain why solar irradiance is divided by four. Use albedo 0.3 and turn Greenhouse off. Read the surface temperature.

steps.title: Tinker
steps.body: Turn Greenhouse on; distinguish surface emission from outgoing radiation at the top of the atmosphere. Check the top-of-atmosphere balance.

steps.title: Explain
steps.body: Explain why a change in reflected sunlight or infrared absorption changes the temperature needed for energy balance.

steps.title: Check
steps.body: Choose an answer and explain your reasoning. Each question includes feedback.

questions.prompt: What hits the ground first from the Sun?
questions.explain: The Sun's high temperature produces radiation mainly at shorter wavelengths than Earth's thermal emission. After absorbing energy, the much cooler surface emits mainly longwave infrared radiation.

choices: The fraction of incoming shortwave a surface reflects
questions.explain: Albedo compares reflected shortwave energy with incoming shortwave energy. A high-albedo surface reflects a larger fraction and absorbs less of the incident sunlight.

questions.prompt: Why can a snowy Cairngorm plateau heat the air less than bare peat?
choices: Higher albedo, so less absorbed shortwave.
questions.explain: Snow usually reflects a larger fraction of incoming sunlight than dark peat, leaving less energy available for surface heating. Melting and evaporation can further change how absorbed energy is partitioned.

questions.prompt: Greenhouse return in this lab is…
choices: Thermal radiation emitted by the atmosphere towards the surface.
questions.explain: Greenhouse gases and clouds absorb and emit infrared radiation, including radiation directed downwards. This downward thermal flux adds to the surface energy budget while the surface also emits energy upwards.

why: Earth reflects some incoming sunlight and absorbs the rest. Its temperature adjusts as outgoing thermal radiation balances absorbed energy; greenhouse gases change the exchange of thermal radiation.
Turn Greenhouse on; distinguish surface emission from outgoing radiation at the top of the atmosphere. Check the top-of-atmosphere balance.
This simple energy-balance model isolates selected processes rather than representing the full atmosphere and climate system.

glossary.def: The fraction of incoming sunlight reflected by a surface, expressed from zero to one or as a percentage. Fresh snow usually has a high albedo and dark soil a lower one. Reflected energy in watts per square metre is a flux, not albedo itself.

Radiation at the shorter wavelengths that carry most incoming solar energy, including visible light and parts of the ultraviolet and infrared spectrum. Earth’s much cooler surface emits mainly longwave radiation instead. Shortwave does not mean visible light alone.

Thermal infrared radiation emitted by Earth’s surface and atmosphere. It generally has longer wavelengths than most incoming solar radiation. Greenhouse gases absorb and emit parts of this spectrum, influencing the rate at which energy escapes to space.
Warming of a planet's surface and lower atmosphere because gases and clouds absorb and emit thermal infrared radiation, affecting the loss of energy to space.

An accounting of energy entering and leaving a system, such as Earth or a patch of ground. A persistent imbalance changes stored energy and can cause warming or cooling. A surface budget also includes evaporation and sensible heat transfers.

The transfer of radiation into a material, increasing its internal energy. Dark ground often absorbs more sunlight than bright snow. Absorption differs from reflection, which sends radiation away, and transmission, which lets it pass through.

The release of radiation by matter. Earth’s surface and atmosphere emit thermal infrared radiation at temperatures typical of this planet. This differs from reflection, which redirects incoming radiation without first absorbing it.

Incoming solar radiation received at a surface. Its amount depends on the angle of the Sun, daylight duration and atmospheric conditions. Insolation is an energy input; air temperature also depends on energy losses, storage and transport.

misconception.claim: Greenhouse gases mainly warm Earth by trapping incoming visible sunlight.
misconception.truth: Much incoming solar radiation reaches the surface, where some is absorbed. The warmed surface emits thermal infrared radiation, which greenhouse gases and clouds absorb and emit. This exchange changes the surface temperature needed for the Earth system to balance absorbed solar energy with energy leaving for space.

misconceptions.claim: Greenhouse gases mainly warm Earth by trapping incoming visible sunlight.
misconceptions.truth: Much incoming solar radiation reaches the surface, where some is absorbed. The warmed surface emits thermal infrared radiation, which greenhouse gases and clouds absorb and emit. This exchange changes the surface temperature needed for the Earth system to balance absorbed solar energy with energy leaving for space.

teacher.script:
Explain why solar irradiance is divided by four. Use albedo 0.3 and turn Greenhouse off. Read the surface temperature.

Turn Greenhouse on; distinguish surface emission from outgoing radiation at the top of the atmosphere. Check the top-of-atmosphere balance.
pitfalls: Distinguish the model’s energy transfers from a prediction of future climate.
Explain albedo as the fraction of incoming sunlight reflected, and distinguish shortwave sunlight from outgoing longwave radiation.
Use only the energy values supplied by the model when comparing transfers or checking a budget.

sources.label: University of Washington one-layer radiation balance

modelNotes: Averaging 1361 W/m² over the globe gives 340.25 W/m² before reflection.
With Greenhouse on, infrared absorptivity and emissivity are both 0.78.

labs.title: Thermal circulation
labs.hook: Unequal heating can create pressure differences and a circulation.
labs.objective: Explain how unequal heating creates a circulation, then apply that reasoning to a coastal breeze and an urban heat island.

steps.title: Observe
steps.body: Compare sea and land at local hour 15. Trace surface inflow towards the warmer land and return flow aloft.

steps.title: Tinker
steps.body: Scrub to hour 3 and identify the possible reversal. Select Urban heat and compare city with rural surroundings.

steps.title: Explain
steps.body: How does the temperature contrast between land and sea produce a circulation that may reverse overnight?

steps.title: Check
steps.body: Choose an answer and explain your reasoning. Each question includes feedback.

questions.prompt: A sea breeze at the surface blows…
questions.explain: During the day, land commonly warms faster than the adjacent sea, helping air rise over the land. The resulting pressure differences can draw cooler surface air inland as a sea breeze.

questions.prompt: At night the land often cools faster. The surface flow…
choices: Can reverse as a land breeze
questions.explain: If land cools below the sea's temperature at night, the local pressure pattern can reverse and drive surface air offshore. Background winds and cloud cover can weaken or prevent this land breeze.

choices: A city that stays warmer, especially at night, because of surface materials and less evaporative cooling.
questions.explain: Urban materials store and release heat, while reduced vegetation often limits evaporative cooling. These changes can keep a city warmer than its surroundings, especially at night.

questions.prompt: Why does this local experiment omit Coriolis?
choices: Coriolis is exactly zero over all coasts.
To isolate thermal forcing; rotation can still affect real breezes.
The sea does not rotate with Earth.
Pressure differences are impossible near the coast.
questions.explain: Removing Coriolis allows this experiment to isolate circulation driven by local heating contrasts. Real breezes also respond to Earth's rotation, background winds and the surrounding terrain.

why: Unequal heating can create pressure differences and a circulation. Warm air expands and rises relative to its surroundings, with return flow completing the circulation at another level.
Scrub to hour 3 and identify the possible reversal. Select Urban heat and compare city with rural surroundings.
The illustrated circulation isolates differential heating; real winds also depend on rotation, friction and surrounding weather systems.

glossary.def: A local wind blowing from sea towards land when daytime heating makes the land warmer than nearby water. A circulation develops with rising air over land and return flow aloft. Stronger background winds can weaken or overwhelm it.
A local wind from land towards the sea, commonly at night when land has cooled faster. Larger-scale winds can weaken or prevent it.
An urban area that is warmer than nearby surroundings, often most evident at night. Surface materials, reduced evaporation, urban geometry and waste heat contribute.

A circulation driven by differences in heating and the resulting pressure and density patterns. A sea breeze is a local example, with rising air over warmer land. Rotation and background winds alter larger-scale circulation.
Air moving from the sea towards land. It can occur in a local sea breeze or within a larger weather system. The term describes direction relative to the coast, not a fixed compass bearing.
A difference in pressure between two places. It creates a pressure-gradient force that can start air moving.

Cooling that occurs when evaporation uses energy from a surface and its surroundings. A moist surface can lose energy as latent heat instead of warming. The effect depends on available water, humidity, wind and incoming energy.

misconception.claim: A sea breeze always blows from sea to land, by day and by night.
misconception.truth: A daytime sea breeze can develop when land warms faster than nearby water, creating a circulation with onshore flow near the surface. Overnight cooling may support a land breeze in the opposite direction. Background winds, clouds and coastal terrain can weaken or prevent either circulation.

misconceptions.claim: A sea breeze always blows from sea to land, by day and by night.
misconceptions.truth: A daytime sea breeze can develop when land warms faster than nearby water, creating a circulation with onshore flow near the surface. Overnight cooling may support a land breeze in the opposite direction. Background winds, clouds and coastal terrain can weaken or prevent either circulation.

teacher.script:
Compare sea and land at local hour 15. Trace surface inflow towards the warmer land and return flow aloft.

Scrub to hour 3 and identify the possible reversal. Select Urban heat and compare city with rural surroundings.
pitfalls: Treat the selected land and sea temperatures as experimental inputs rather than observations from a particular coast.
Explain that local temperature contrasts favour breezes, while larger weather systems can change or suppress them.
Discuss the scale of the circulation rather than claiming that Coriolis becomes exactly zero in a local setting.

modelNotes: The displayed loop is enlarged vertically fourfold; Physical scale restores the conceptual domain’s 20 km width and 2 km depth.

labs.title: Wind, PGF and Coriolis
labs.hook: Air accelerates in response to pressure differences.
labs.objective: Explain how pressure differences start air moving and how Earth’s rotation and surface friction change its direction.

steps.title: Observe
steps.body: Identify the lower-pressure side and predict the pressure-gradient arrow. Compare north and south hemispheres at steady balance.

steps.title: Tinker
steps.body: Add friction and describe the cross-isobar component. Select Release from rest and scrub Process.

steps.title: Explain
steps.body: Why does adding friction change both the speed and direction of the wind?

steps.title: Check
steps.body: Choose an answer and explain your reasoning. Each question includes feedback.

questions.explain: A pressure difference exerts a net force from higher towards lower pressure. A steeper pressure gradient produces a stronger force per unit mass of air.

questions.prompt: In the northern hemisphere Coriolis deflects…
questions.explain: In the rotating Earth frame, Coriolis deflects horizontal motion to its right in the Northern Hemisphere. The deflection is relative to the direction of travel, not always towards a fixed compass direction.

questions.prompt: Friction near the surface makes wind…
questions.explain: Surface friction slows the wind and weakens its Coriolis deflection. The pressure-gradient force then gives the flow a component across the isobars towards lower pressure.

questions.prompt: The horizontal Coriolis parameter f is zero at…
questions.explain: For horizontal motion, the Coriolis parameter is proportional to the sine of latitude. It is zero at the equator and changes sign between the two hemispheres.

why: Air accelerates in response to pressure differences. Earth’s rotation deflects its motion, while surface friction changes both wind speed and the angle at which it crosses pressure contours.
Add friction and describe the cross-isobar component. Select Release from rest and scrub Process.
The selected pressure field and drag isolate these forces; changing a slider is not a prediction of wind at a real location.

glossary.def: An apparent acceleration in a rotating reference frame. For horizontal motion on Earth it deflects flow right in the Northern Hemisphere and left in the Southern; that horizontal component vanishes at the equator.
Pressure-gradient force: the force per unit mass associated with a pressure difference, directed from higher towards lower pressure.

An idealised wind in which the pressure-gradient force is balanced by Coriolis acceleration, so flow runs parallel to straight isobars. It is most useful above the frictional surface layer and away from the equator.

Drag between moving air and the surface, which slows the wind and changes its direction. Near the ground this allows wind to cross isobars towards lower pressure. Higher in the atmosphere, surface friction is much weaker.

A line joining places with the same atmospheric pressure on a weather chart. Closely spaced isobars indicate a large pressure gradient over a given distance. Wind also responds to Earth’s rotation and friction, so it does not simply follow that gradient.
With your back to the wind in the Northern Hemisphere, lower pressure generally lies to your left; the relation reverses in the Southern Hemisphere. Surface friction modifies the angle.

The change in atmospheric pressure over a given distance. A larger gradient exerts a stronger pressure-gradient force on air. Closely spaced isobars often indicate a strong gradient, but wind also depends on friction and Earth’s rotation.

misconception.claim: Wind always blows straight from high pressure to low pressure.
misconception.truth: The pressure-gradient force accelerates air towards lower pressure, while Earth’s rotation deflects moving air and friction affects flow near the surface. Their combined effects determine wind direction. Winds aloft can run approximately along isobars, while surface winds commonly cross them towards lower pressure.

misconceptions.claim: Wind always blows straight from high pressure to low pressure.
misconceptions.truth: The pressure-gradient force accelerates air towards lower pressure, while Earth’s rotation deflects moving air and friction affects flow near the surface. Their combined effects determine wind direction. Winds aloft can run approximately along isobars, while surface winds commonly cross them towards lower pressure.

teacher.script:
Identify the lower-pressure side and predict the pressure-gradient arrow. Compare north and south hemispheres at steady balance.

Add friction and describe the cross-isobar component. Select Release from rest and scrub Process.
pitfalls: Explain Coriolis as an apparent deflection in Earth’s rotating reference frame and check the direction in each hemisphere.
Use large-scale atmospheric examples rather than sinks or toilets to demonstrate the Coriolis effect.
Distinguish the pressure-gradient force that accelerates air from friction that slows it and changes its direction.

modelNotes: The fixed northward pressure-gradient acceleration is 0.001 m/s².
Coriolis parameter f is ±0.0001 s⁻¹; surface friction uses a linear drag coefficient of 0.00005 s⁻¹.
Select Release from rest and Play or scrub Process to see the first 24 hours.

labs.title: Three-cell circulation
labs.hook: Unequal solar heating and Earth’s rotation organise broad atmospheric circulation.
labs.objective: Locate the Hadley, Ferrel and polar cells and relate their circulation to broad patterns of winds and rainfall.

steps.title: Observe
steps.body: Identify Hadley, Ferrel and Polar in the zonal-mean view. Follow near-surface easterlies and westerlies.

steps.title: Tinker
steps.body: Distinguish the eddy-driven Ferrel circulation from a thermally direct cell. Play the illustrative annual shift; explain why real ITCZ positions differ.

steps.title: Explain
steps.body: How do rising and sinking air help explain broad rainfall patterns, and why does the Ferrel cell need a different explanation?

steps.title: Check
steps.body: Choose an answer and explain your reasoning. Each question includes feedback.

questions.prompt: The Hadley cell has rising air near…
questions.explain: Strong tropical heating and surface convergence support rising air near the ITCZ. This ascent forms the rising branch of the idealised Hadley circulation.

choices: Seasonal heating and land–ocean contrasts move the zone of convergence.
questions.explain: Seasonal changes in heating and differences between land and ocean shift the zone where tropical surface winds converge. Its position varies with longitude and does not simply follow the latitude directly beneath the Sun.

questions.prompt: Ferrel cell is called indirect because…
choices: The mean cell is maintained mainly by midlatitude eddy transports.
questions.explain: Midlatitude weather systems transport heat and momentum and help maintain the mean Ferrel circulation. Its mean rising and sinking branches oppose the pattern expected from direct local heating alone.

questions.prompt: Why does Earth differ from a simple one-cell circulation?
choices: Rotation and weather eddies alter heat and momentum transport, producing a more complex mean circulation.
questions.explain: Earth's rotation constrains large-scale motion, while weather systems redistribute heat and momentum. Their combined effects produce a circulation more complex than a single direct equator-to-pole loop.

why: Unequal solar heating and Earth’s rotation organise broad atmospheric circulation. Rising and sinking regions help explain the trade winds, westerlies and major pressure belts.
Distinguish the eddy-driven Ferrel circulation from a thermally direct cell. Play the illustrative annual shift; explain why real ITCZ positions differ.
The three-cell pattern is an average framework; actual circulation shifts with seasons, continents and changing weather.

glossary.def: The average tropical circulation in which air rises near the equatorial convergence zone, moves poleward aloft and descends in the subtropics. Near-surface return flow contributes to the trade winds. The real circulation shifts with seasons and continents.
The mean midlatitude atmospheric circulation, with poleward near-surface flow and equatorward flow aloft. It is an indirect cell maintained largely by weather systems.

The average circulation in which cold air sinks near a pole and moves equatorward near the surface, returning poleward aloft. It forms part of a simplified global circulation model. Actual polar weather is less uniform than a single closed loop.
The intertropical convergence zone: a shifting belt where tropical trade winds meet and moist air often rises. Its position varies with season, oceans and land heating.

The prevailing tropical surface winds blowing towards the equatorial convergence zone. Earth’s rotation gives them an easterly component: they generally come from the northeast in the Northern Hemisphere and southeast in the Southern Hemisphere. Their position and strength vary seasonally.

A region of relatively high atmospheric pressure commonly found near the poleward side of the Hadley circulation. Descending air tends to suppress cloud formation, helping explain many subtropical dry regions. Its position and strength vary with season and geography.
A belt of the highest mean temperatures at a given season. It shifts with seasonal heating and geography and does not always coincide with the geographic equator or ITCZ.

The prevailing winds with a west-to-east component across much of the middle latitudes. They help steer many weather systems, although individual winds change as pressure systems move. Their average pattern reflects atmospheric circulation and Earth’s rotation.

misconception.claim: The three atmospheric cells are fixed loops followed by individual air parcels.
misconception.truth: The three-cell model describes broad averages of circulation across latitude. Real air moves through changing weather systems and mixes between regions. Continents, seasons and ocean conditions disturb the pattern, and the midlatitude Ferrel circulation is maintained largely by weather systems rather than a simple isolated convection loop.

misconceptions.claim: The three atmospheric cells are fixed loops followed by individual air parcels.
misconceptions.truth: The three-cell model describes broad averages of circulation across latitude. Real air moves through changing weather systems and mixes between regions. Continents, seasons and ocean conditions disturb the pattern, and the midlatitude Ferrel circulation is maintained largely by weather systems rather than a simple isolated convection loop.

teacher.script:
Identify Hadley, Ferrel and Polar in the zonal-mean view. Follow near-surface easterlies and westerlies.

Distinguish the eddy-driven Ferrel circulation from a thermally direct cell. Play the illustrative annual shift; explain why real ITCZ positions differ.
pitfalls: Use the three-cell model as a broad circulation pattern rather than three equal, fixed cells.
Locate the United Kingdom in the midlatitudes rather than in the Hadley cell, and allow the ITCZ to shift seasonally.
Explain that the Ferrel cell is an indirect circulation influenced by midlatitude weather systems.

modelNotes: Play a year to move a prescribed ITCZ between 10° S and 10° N.
T reduces the displayed cell depth to 12 km against a 6371 km Earth radius.

labs.title: Fronts as wedges
labs.hook: A weather front separates air masses with different temperature and density.
labs.objective: Compare warm, cold and occluded fronts, and explain how the movement of contrasting air masses produces cloud and rain.

steps.title: Observe
steps.body: Identify cold air, the warm sector and cool air ahead. Compare the two prescribed slopes.

steps.title: Tinker
steps.body: Scrub Process to 0.70, where the surface warm sector closes. Continue and locate warm air above the meeting point.

steps.title: Explain
steps.body: Explain how the slopes and motion of contrasting air masses affect where warm air rises.

steps.title: Check
steps.body: Choose an answer and explain your reasoning. Each question includes feedback.

choices: A wedge of colder air undercutting warmer air
questions.explain: Advancing cold air is denser than the warmer air ahead and pushes beneath it. The forced ascent can produce cloud and precipitation along a relatively steep frontal boundary.

choices: A gentler slope, cloud thickening ahead
questions.explain: At a warm front, advancing warm air gradually rises over a retreating colder air mass. Its gentler slope often spreads cloud and precipitation over a broader area ahead of the surface front.

choices: Cold front catches the warm front; warm air is lifted off the surface
questions.explain: An occlusion develops when a cold front catches a warm front and lifts the warm sector away from the ground. The resulting structure depends on the temperatures of the two colder air masses.

questions.prompt: The line on a Met Office chart is…
choices: The whole front, vertical from ground to space
The surface trace of a sloping wedge; the weather sits on the slope
A painted television graphic with no height
questions.explain: A weather-map front marks where the sloping boundary between air masses meets Earth's surface. Cloud and precipitation can extend well away from that line because air is lifted along the boundary above it.

why: A weather front separates air masses with different temperature and density. A colder air mass can undercut warmer air, while a warm front rises more gradually over cold air ahead.
Scrub Process to 0.70, where the surface warm sector closes. Continue and locate warm air above the meeting point.
The chosen front slopes and speeds illustrate their geometry; cloud shapes do not calculate rainfall totals.

glossary.def: The advancing boundary of a colder air mass that displaces warmer air. Uplift near the front can produce cloud and rain, with weather depending on moisture and stability.

The boundary where a warmer air mass advances over colder air near the surface. Gradual uplift can produce extensive layered cloud and precipitation. The exact weather depends on moisture, stability and the larger storm system.

The process in which a cold front catches up with a warm front and lifts the intervening warm air away from the surface. The resulting occluded front can have extensive cloud and precipitation, depending on the air masses involved.
The milder air between the warm front and the cold front in a midlatitude cyclone.

In the fronts lab, the line where a sloping boundary between air masses meets Earth’s surface. It is plotted using weather observations. The edge of a visible cloud band may lie elsewhere and does not locate the front precisely.
A large body of air with broadly similar temperature and moisture characteristics acquired over a source region.
A narrow, often violent band of convection, commonly along or ahead of a cold front.

misconception.claim: A front is a solid wall that keeps two air masses completely separate.
misconception.truth: A front is a transition zone across which properties such as temperature and humidity change. Its slope and movement affect how air is lifted, with cloud and precipitation depending on moisture and stability. Mixing occurs, and real fronts have more complex shapes than a single dividing line.

misconceptions.claim: A front is a solid wall that keeps two air masses completely separate.
misconceptions.truth: A front is a transition zone across which properties such as temperature and humidity change. Its slope and movement affect how air is lifted, with cloud and precipitation depending on moisture and stability. Mixing occurs, and real fronts have more complex shapes than a single dividing line.

teacher.script:
Identify cold air, the warm sector and cool air ahead. Compare the two prescribed slopes.

Scrub Process to 0.70, where the surface warm sector closes. Continue and locate warm air above the meeting point.
pitfalls: Use the three-dimensional slope of a front to explain cloud and rainfall patterns beyond its line on a map.
Compare the slopes of warm and cold fronts without drawing either as a perfectly vertical wall.
Distinguish rainbands associated with midlatitude fronts from the structure of a tropical cyclone.

modelNotes: The experiment prescribes a cold-front slope of 1:50 and a gentler warm-front slope of 1:150 across 600 km.

labs.title: Cyclone and anticyclone
labs.hook: Around a low-pressure system, air tends to converge near the surface; around a high it tends to diverge.
labs.objective: Compare pressure and airflow around a cyclone and an anticyclone, then relate each pattern to the weather it can bring.

steps.title: Observe
steps.body: Identify the low and trace surface convergence. Read spin from above, then reverse hemisphere.

steps.title: Tinker
steps.body: Switch to Anticyclone and distinguish divergence from rotation. Name the exaggerated vertical motion.

steps.title: Explain
steps.body: How do surface convergence and divergence differ from the rotation around a pressure system?

steps.title: Check
steps.body: Choose an answer and explain your reasoning. Each question includes feedback.

questions.prompt: In the northern hemisphere a midlatitude cyclone spins…
questions.explain: The pressure-gradient force draws air towards the low, while Northern Hemisphere Coriolis deflection acts to the right of its motion. The resulting circulation is anticlockwise, with surface friction adding inward flow.

choices: A surface low and rising air
A surface high and sinking air, often clearer skies
questions.explain: Air commonly descends within an anticyclone and warms as it is compressed, reducing relative humidity. Clearer skies are common, although low cloud or fog can persist beneath an inversion.

Most UK winter depressions develop in midlatitudes along strong horizontal temperature contrasts and have fronts. Tropical cyclones draw much of their energy from warm-ocean heat and moisture and have a different structure.

questions.prompt: Clockwise surface flow around a high in the northern hemisphere is…
choices: An anticyclone: high, sinking, often clearer
questions.explain: In the Northern Hemisphere, the pressure-gradient force points away from a high and Coriolis deflects the moving air to its right. The resulting anticyclonic circulation is clockwise, with outward flow near the surface.

why: Around a low-pressure system, air tends to converge near the surface; around a high it tends to diverge. Rotation and friction determine the circulation direction and cross-isobar flow.
Switch to Anticyclone and distinguish divergence from rotation. Name the exaggerated vertical motion.
These idealised pressure systems show circulation patterns; cloud and rainfall depend on moisture and stability as well as pressure.

glossary.def: A circulation around a low-pressure centre: anticlockwise in the Northern Hemisphere and clockwise in the Southern. Tropical and extratropical cyclones form through different processes.

An atmospheric circulation around a region of high pressure, commonly associated with sinking air. Surface winds turn clockwise in the Northern Hemisphere and anticlockwise in the Southern Hemisphere. Clear skies are common, but fog and low cloud can persist.
In meteorology, a region of low atmospheric pressure; in UK usage, commonly an extratropical cyclone.

The movement of air towards an area, bringing neighbouring flows together. Near the surface it can encourage rising air, cloud and rain if enough moisture is present. Convergence describes a flow pattern; it is not itself a type of cloud.

The spreading of air away from an area. Surface divergence commonly accompanies sinking air in high-pressure systems, while divergence aloft can help sustain rising air below. Always state the height at which the flow is diverging.
A curved, comma-like cloud pattern often seen in satellite views of developing or mature extratropical cyclones.
Outside the tropics. An extratropical cyclone is a storm system usually associated with fronts and horizontal temperature contrasts.

misconception.claim: High pressure always brings hot, sunny weather.
misconception.truth: High pressure is commonly associated with descending air, but surface weather also depends on season, moisture and temperature. An anticyclone can bring clear skies or persistent fog and low cloud. In winter, weak winds and clear nights can allow strong cooling near the ground.

misconceptions.claim: High pressure always brings hot, sunny weather.
misconceptions.truth: High pressure is commonly associated with descending air, but surface weather also depends on season, moisture and temperature. An anticyclone can bring clear skies or persistent fog and low cloud. In winter, weak winds and clear nights can allow strong cooling near the ground.

teacher.script:
Identify the low and trace surface convergence. Read spin from above, then reverse hemisphere.

Switch to Anticyclone and distinguish divergence from rotation. Name the exaggerated vertical motion.
pitfalls: Check the hemisphere before describing the direction of circulation around high and low pressure.
Distinguish a midlatitude cyclone with fronts from a tropical cyclone driven by warm-ocean conditions.
Explain that an anticyclone can bring fog or low cloud, so high pressure does not guarantee sunshine.

labs.title: Climate types
labs.hook: Compare the world’s climate families through long-term temperature and rainfall patterns.
labs.objective: Explore the five major climate families and explain how long-term temperature and rainfall patterns shape their global distribution.

steps.title: Observe
steps.body: Read the A–E legend and identify the highlighted family on the globe.

steps.title: Tinker
steps.body: Choose Tropical, then Dry. Compare their distribution and explain why temperature alone cannot separate them.

steps.title: Explain
steps.body: Why must rainfall be considered alongside temperature when comparing tropical and dry climates?

steps.title: Check
steps.body: Choose an answer and explain your reasoning. Each question includes feedback.

choices: Long-term monthly temperature and precipitation patterns.
Only the plants visible in one photograph.
questions.explain: Köppen–Geiger classes use thresholds based on long-term monthly temperature and precipitation, including their seasonal distribution. Vegetation is related to those conditions but is not itself the measured input defining each class.

choices: Dry and either hot or cold.
A guarantee of rain every day.
questions.explain: The B family is identified by an aridity threshold that depends on temperature and precipitation seasonality. A separate distinction identifies hot and cold dry climates.

questions.prompt: The London Cfb reference applies to…
choices: Every location in the United Kingdom.
A sampled reference point in a specified dataset and period.
Only the hottest day ever recorded.
questions.explain: A climate label describes the data at the sampled location over the selected reference period. Other places in the same country can fall into different classes because of elevation, coastal influence or regional rainfall patterns.

choices: Only landscapes covered by permanent ice.
Every place with a cold winter.
Only locations in the Southern Hemisphere.
questions.explain: Both tundra and ice-cap climates have a warmest-month mean below 10 °C. Tundra reaches at least 0 °C in its warmest month, while an ice-cap climate remains below 0 °C.

why: Köppen–Geiger groups climates using long-term monthly temperature and rainfall. Tropical, dry, temperate, continental and polar families describe different combinations of warmth, seasonality and moisture.
Select a family below the globe, then rotate Earth to compare where it occurs. The marked city gives one local example; nearby coasts and highlands may have a different class.
The colours summarise the 1991–2020 reference period; a location’s climate class does not determine its current weather or exact vegetation.

glossary.def: A climate classification system that groups places by long-term monthly temperature and precipitation. Its letter codes describe climatic thresholds and seasonality. Vegetation can suggest a climate, but one landscape or one day’s weather cannot determine the classification.
A large ecological region characterised by its vegetation and associated organisms, influenced strongly by climate, soils and disturbance.
Köppen temperate oceanic climate, with no dry season and warm rather than hot summers. London is a familiar example.
Köppen hot desert climate: precipitation falls below the desert aridity threshold and mean annual temperature is at least 18 °C.
Köppen tropical rainforest climate: every month averages at least 18 °C and receives at least 60 mm of precipitation.

The influence of distance from the ocean on a place’s climate. Inland locations often have larger seasonal temperature ranges because land heats and cools faster than water. Prevailing winds, elevation and nearby currents also affect the contrast.
The statistical pattern of weather over a long period, commonly 30 years, including averages, seasonal variation and extremes.

misconception.claim: One unusual day of weather can change a place’s climate classification.
misconception.truth: Climate classifications use long-term patterns, such as monthly temperature and precipitation statistics. A heatwave or wet day is an event within that distribution. Classifying a place therefore requires a representative record, while a longer-lasting shift in the statistics may eventually change its classification.

misconceptions.claim: One unusual day of weather can change a place’s climate classification.
misconceptions.truth: Climate classifications use long-term patterns, such as monthly temperature and precipitation statistics. A heatwave or wet day is an event within that distribution. Classifying a place therefore requires a representative record, while a longer-lasting shift in the statistics may eventually change its classification.

teacher.script:
Choose Tropical and ask students to describe where it occurs. Then choose Dry and discuss why rainfall matters as well as temperature.

Locate London as a temperate example, then compare Helsinki and Nuuk. Ask students why a city’s classification should not be assigned to its whole country.

Finish by distinguishing climate from today’s weather. Discuss why vegetation also depends on soil, land use and disturbance, then use Check to test the explanation.
pitfalls: Use long-term temperature and rainfall patterns to explain climate classes rather than treating them as today’s weather.
Keep a reference point’s climate separate from the range of climates found across a whole country.
Explain that a climate family can support several vegetation types and does not determine one unique biome.

labs.title: Drainage basin
labs.hook: A drainage basin collects water that flows towards a common outlet.
labs.objective: Trace water through a drainage basin and explain how the watershed connects the tributaries to a shared outlet.

steps.title: Observe
steps.body: Show the drainage divide and trace the edge of the basin. Identify which slopes drain towards the same outlet.

steps.title: Tinker
steps.body: Follow a tributary to its confluence with the main river. Hide the labels and ask a partner to locate the source, confluence and mouth.

steps.title: Explain
steps.body: How does the drainage divide determine which slopes supply water to the same river outlet?

steps.title: Check
steps.body: Choose an answer and explain your reasoning. Each question includes feedback.

questions.explain: The drainage divide follows higher ground separating surface runoff that reaches different river systems. It forms the outer boundary of the selected basin.
A confluence is the meeting point of two or more river channels. Their flows combine and continue downstream in a shared channel.

choices: Where the river meets sea, lake, or a larger river
questions.explain: The mouth is the downstream end where a river enters another body of water. Whether a delta develops there depends on sediment supply and how rapidly waves, tides or currents redistribute it.

choices: Only the blue channel on the map
The whole hillside that drains to this river, bounded by the divide
questions.explain: Rain falling on basin slopes can reach the river by surface runoff, soil flow or groundwater flow. The drainage basin therefore includes the contributing land as well as the visible channels.

why: A drainage basin collects water that flows towards a common outlet. The watershed separates it from neighbouring basins; tributaries connect hillslope inputs to the main river.
Follow a tributary to its confluence with the main river. Hide the labels and ask a partner to locate the source, confluence and mouth.
The terrain is a teaching catchment, and the flow traces show routes rather than measured travel times.

glossary.def: In UK geography, the drainage divide separating basins. In US usage, watershed commonly means the entire drainage basin; check the context.
The area of land drained by a river and its tributaries, bounded by the watershed.

The starting point of a river’s channel, which may be a spring, a lake outlet or the convergence of small flows. The river also receives water along its course, so its source is not its only water input.

A stream or river that joins a larger channel at a confluence. Its flow and sediment contribute to the downstream river. A tributary can have its own drainage basin nested within the larger river system.

The place where two streams or rivers meet. Downstream discharge usually includes water from both channels, although its timing depends on travel and storage. Sediment bars and mixing patterns may reveal the different flows at the junction.

The place where a river enters a sea, lake or another river. Its form depends on sediment supply, water movement and local topography. Some mouths build deltas, while others form tidal estuaries or enter a larger channel directly.

Higher ground between neighbouring river valleys or channels. Its slopes shed water towards the adjacent channels. An interfluve may lie within a larger drainage basin and is not necessarily the boundary of that entire basin.

misconception.claim: All rain falling within a drainage basin reaches its river immediately.
misconception.truth: Rainfall can be intercepted, infiltrate soil, replenish groundwater, evaporate or enter surface runoff. These pathways have different travel times, and some water remains stored or leaves through evapotranspiration. The river’s response depends on both rainfall and the basin’s existing conditions.

misconceptions.truth: Rainfall can be intercepted, infiltrate soil, replenish groundwater, evaporate or enter surface runoff. These pathways have different travel times, and some water remains stored or leaves through evapotranspiration. The river’s response depends on both rainfall and the basin’s existing conditions.
