Show the drainage divide and trace the edge of the basin. Identify which slopes drain towards the same outlet.

Follow a tributary to its confluence with the main river. Hide the labels and ask a partner to locate the source, confluence and mouth.
pitfalls: Trace the full land area draining towards the outlet, not only the river channels.
Clarify whether watershed means the drainage divide or the whole basin in the terminology being used.
Distinguish the river mouth from a delta, which forms only where sediment accumulates under suitable conditions.

modelNotes: Vertical exaggeration is labelled ×8 so the bowl reads from the back of the room; a real Thames divide can be a low ridge or a field boundary, not a crater rim.
Orbit the bowl; it is a 3D catchment, not a 2D paint fill.
Without the 3D view: a rim, a source, tributaries joining at a confluence, a mouth.

labs.title: Storm hydrograph
labs.hook: A storm hydrograph shows how river discharge changes after rainfall.
labs.objective: Read the main features of a storm hydrograph and explain how urban surfaces can change the timing and size of peak discharge.

steps.title: Observe
steps.body: Play the storm and compare rainfall with the rising and falling limbs of river discharge. Locate the rainfall and discharge peaks.

steps.title: Tinker
steps.body: Increase Urban cover and compare peak discharge and lag time. Return to a less urban catchment and explain how infiltration and storage change the response.

steps.title: Explain
steps.body: Why does the discharge peak occur after the rainfall peak, and how can urban cover change that delay?

steps.title: Check
steps.body: Choose an answer and explain your reasoning. Each question includes feedback.

questions.explain: In this lab, lag time is the interval between peak rainfall intensity and peak discharge. Water takes time to move through the catchment and reach the measurement point.
Paved surfaces reduce infiltration, while drains can carry runoff rapidly to channels. Under comparable rainfall, these changes commonly raise the flood peak and shorten its lag.
On the falling limb, discharge decreases after its peak as readily available runoff is exhausted. Slower drainage from soil and groundwater can sustain the remaining flow.

choices: The same number with two names
Height of the water surface versus volume of water per time — do not mix them
questions.explain: Stage measures water-surface height relative to a reference level, whereas discharge measures volume passing a section per unit time. The relationship depends on the channel and cannot be transferred unchanged between different sites.

why: A storm hydrograph shows how river discharge changes after rainfall. Infiltration, storage and routing delay the response; a greater runoff fraction can produce a higher and earlier peak.
Increase Urban cover and compare peak discharge and lag time. Return to a less urban catchment and explain how infiltration and storage change the response.
The calculation uses an invented catchment and prescribed storm so you can compare processes without treating the curve as a local forecast.

glossary.def: A graph showing how river discharge or water level changes with time. A storm hydrograph may be shown alongside a separate rainfall graph to compare timing and response.
The delay between a rainfall reference, commonly peak rainfall, and peak river discharge. State the convention used when reading a storm hydrograph.

The part of a hydrograph during which river discharge increases towards a peak. Its steepness reflects how quickly water reaches the channel. A rapid rise can follow intense rain or efficient runoff from saturated or paved surfaces.
The greatest rate of river flow during a specified event or period, measured in m³ s⁻¹.

The part of a hydrograph after its peak, when discharge decreases as stored water drains from a catchment. Its shape reflects delayed flow from soil, groundwater and channels. Rain may have stopped well before river discharge returns to its earlier level.
The sustained part of river discharge supplied mainly by groundwater and other delayed stores between rainfall events.

The height of a river’s water surface above a specified gauge datum. Stage can be converted to discharge using a calibrated rating relationship, but they are different measurements. Changes in the channel can alter that relationship.
The volume of water passing a river cross-section per unit time, usually measured in m³ s⁻¹. For mean velocity v and cross-sectional area A, Q = Av.

misconception.claim: Peak river discharge occurs at exactly the same time as peak rainfall.
misconception.truth: Water takes time to move through a catchment and its stores, so the discharge peak commonly follows the rainfall peak. The delay depends on rainfall location and duration, catchment size, slopes, soil conditions and drainage. State which rainfall reference is used when measuring lag time.

misconceptions.claim: Peak river discharge occurs at exactly the same time as peak rainfall.
misconceptions.truth: Water takes time to move through a catchment and its stores, so the discharge peak commonly follows the rainfall peak. The delay depends on rainfall location and duration, catchment size, slopes, soil conditions and drainage. State which rainfall reference is used when measuring lag time.

teacher.script:
Play the storm and compare rainfall with the rising and falling limbs of river discharge. Locate the rainfall and discharge peaks.

Increase Urban cover and compare peak discharge and lag time. Return to a less urban catchment and explain how infiltration and storage change the response.
pitfalls: Distinguish river stage, which is a water level, from discharge, which is a volume passing per unit time.
Compare the rainfall peak with the discharge peak and explain the processes that produce a time lag.
Use the timescale of the response to distinguish a rapid flood from a flood with a prolonged recession.

modelNotes: A four-hour triangular storm peaks at 20 mm/h times Rain.
Urban cover raises the runoff fraction from 0.25 to 0.85 and shortens delay and storage time; these are disclosed teaching assumptions, not calibrated site parameters.
The plotted 24-hour window omits part of the long recession; the calculation retains that water in storage.

labs.title: River regime
labs.hook: A river regime describes the seasonal pattern of discharge.
labs.objective: Compare annual patterns of river discharge and explain how rainfall, snowmelt and dams can change their timing.

steps.title: Observe
steps.body: Read the gold and blue annual discharge curves. Scrub through winter and locate water stored as snow.

steps.title: Tinker
steps.body: Follow the melt season and compare its flow peak with winter rain. Switch the dam on and compare the peak and delayed release.

steps.title: Explain
steps.body: How does storing precipitation as snow shift the timing of river flow?

steps.title: Check
steps.body: Choose an answer and explain your reasoning. Each question includes feedback.

questions.prompt: A nival regime is driven by…
questions.explain: A nival regime reflects water stored as seasonal snow and released when temperatures rise. This commonly produces a spring or early-summer increase in discharge rather than an immediate response to winter precipitation.
A pluvial regime is governed mainly by the seasonal distribution of rainfall. Evaporation, soil storage and groundwater can modify when that rainfall appears as river flow.

choices: A continental drain with snowmelt and rain, managed by dams
questions.explain: The Mississippi integrates runoff from a very large basin with contrasting rainfall and snowmelt patterns. Reservoirs, water use and river engineering also modify its seasonal flow.

questions.prompt: A storm hydrograph and a regime graph differ because…
choices: One is hours after a rain pulse; the other is the typical year
questions.explain: A storm hydrograph follows discharge during and after an individual rainfall event, often over hours or days. A regime graph summarises the recurring seasonal pattern, usually using monthly values.

why: A river regime describes the seasonal pattern of discharge. Rain may reach the river quickly, while snow stores water until melting; a reservoir can smooth and delay the resulting flow.
Follow the melt season and compare its flow peak with winter rain. Switch the dam on and compare the peak and delayed release.
Both catchments use invented repeating annual inputs, and the dam represents storage behaviour rather than an actual operating rule.

glossary.def: The characteristic seasonal pattern of river discharge, influenced by rainfall, snowmelt, storage and human regulation.
Describing a river regime strongly influenced by seasonal snowmelt. Discharge often increases during the thawing season. This differs from a glacial regime dominated by the melting of glacier ice.
Describing a river regime mainly controlled by rainfall; its discharge seasonality reflects rainfall and catchment storage.

Water released when accumulated snow changes from solid ice to liquid. Seasonal snowmelt can produce a strong spring or summer rise in river discharge. Its timing depends on temperature, radiation, elevation and snowpack depth.
The volume of water passing a river cross-section per unit time, usually measured in m³ s⁻¹. For mean velocity v and cross-sectional area A, Q = Av.
The sustained part of river discharge supplied mainly by groundwater and other delayed stores between rainfall events.
Changes to a river's discharge timing and magnitude caused by storing and releasing water from a reservoir.

misconception.claim: A river’s seasonal flow pattern depends only on the amount of rain each month.
misconception.truth: Rainfall matters, but snow accumulation and melt, evaporation, groundwater storage and reservoir operation can shift the timing of discharge. Water received in one season may reach the river in another. Explaining a regime therefore requires both the inputs and the processes that delay or remove water.

misconceptions.claim: A river’s seasonal flow pattern depends only on the amount of rain each month.
misconceptions.truth: Rainfall matters, but snow accumulation and melt, evaporation, groundwater storage and reservoir operation can shift the timing of discharge. Water received in one season may reach the river in another. Explaining a regime therefore requires both the inputs and the processes that delay or remove water.

teacher.script:
Read the gold and blue annual discharge curves. Scrub through winter and locate water stored as snow.

Follow the melt season and compare its flow peak with winter rain. Switch the dam on and compare the peak and delayed release.
pitfalls: Compare regimes across different climates rather than applying one annual pattern to every river.
Distinguish a monthly river regime from the short-term response shown by a storm hydrograph.
Use the graph’s stated scale and avoid assigning absolute discharge values to a normalised trace.

modelNotes: These two invented 100 km² catchments use repeating 365-day forcing.
The snow-fed case stores precipitation below 0 °C and melts up to 3 mm water equivalent per positive degree Celsius per day.
Fixed fractions of liquid input, 40% and 25%, are assigned to losses; no detailed evapotranspiration or groundwater model is solved.
The 3D terrain is illustrative, with relief enlarged tenfold until T is pressed; channel width and the dam are symbols.

labs.title: Ocean currents
labs.hook: Surface winds and Earth’s rotation help organise subtropical ocean gyres.
labs.objective: Follow the major surface currents and explain how winds and ocean heat transport contribute to regional climate.

steps.title: Observe
steps.body: Select North Atlantic and identify its western and eastern boundaries. Follow the arrows and name Gulf Stream and Canary Current.

steps.title: Tinker
steps.body: Compare South Atlantic and explain the reversed sense of rotation. Locate all five subtropical gyres.

steps.title: Explain
steps.body: How do winds, Earth’s rotation and ocean-basin boundaries help organise the major surface gyres?

steps.title: Check
steps.body: Choose an answer and explain your reasoning. Each question includes feedback.

choices: A large looping surface current system
questions.explain: A gyre is a broad system of linked ocean currents shaped by wind forcing, Earth's rotation and basin boundaries. Subtropical gyres form large circulating patterns rather than isolated straight streams.

choices: A cold coastal current off Peru
A warm western-boundary current of the North Atlantic
questions.explain: The Gulf Stream carries warm water northwards along the western side of the North Atlantic basin. It is a fast, concentrated boundary current within the wider Atlantic circulation.

choices: A mix of latitude, westerlies, and ocean heat — do not overclaim
questions.explain: Prevailing westerlies bring maritime air towards the UK, and the ocean stores and redistributes heat. Ocean currents contribute to this setting, but UK winter temperatures also depend on atmospheric circulation and latitude.

choices: Narrow, fast and warm on the western side of a subtropical gyre
questions.explain: The variation of Coriolis with latitude concentrates the return flow of a subtropical gyre along its western boundary. This produces relatively narrow, fast currents such as the Gulf Stream and Kuroshio.

why: Surface winds and Earth’s rotation help organise subtropical ocean gyres. Warm western boundary currents generally carry water poleward, while cooler eastern boundary currents carry it towards the equator.
Compare South Atlantic and explain the reversed sense of rotation. Locate all five subtropical gyres.
The globe shows the broad routes and directions of currents; their width and tracer speed are enlarged for reading.

glossary.def: A large-scale rotating system of ocean currents. Winds, Earth’s rotation and the shapes of ocean basins help organise subtropical gyres. A gyre includes currents with different widths, speeds and temperatures rather than one uniform loop.

A narrow, fast current along the western side of an ocean basin’s subtropical gyre, such as the Gulf Stream or Kuroshio. These currents generally carry warm water poleward. Western refers to the ocean basin, not the coast of the neighbouring continent.

A current along the eastern side of an ocean basin, such as the Canary Current. In subtropical gyres these currents are usually broader, slower and cooler than western boundary currents, and coastal winds can also support upwelling.
A fast, warm western-boundary current in the North Atlantic, flowing from the Florida Straits along the eastern United States before turning offshore.

The relatively cool eastern-boundary current flowing southward in the North Atlantic subtropical gyre. Coastal upwelling along northwest Africa can bring colder, nutrient-rich water to the surface. The current is a moving water mass, not simply a strip of cold weather.

A region of relatively high atmospheric pressure commonly found near the poleward side of the Hadley circulation. Descending air tends to suppress cloud formation, helping explain many subtropical dry regions. Its position and strength vary with season and geography.
Flow in the upper ocean, driven by winds and pressure gradients and modified by rotation, coastlines and mixing.

misconception.claim: Ocean currents are driven only by differences in water temperature.
misconception.truth: Winds and pressure gradients drive much upper-ocean circulation, with Earth’s rotation and coastlines shaping the flow. Temperature and salinity affect density and contribute to overturning, while mixing connects different depths. Surface gyres and deep circulation are related but cannot be explained by temperature alone.

misconceptions.claim: Ocean currents are driven only by differences in water temperature.
misconceptions.truth: Winds and pressure gradients drive much upper-ocean circulation, with Earth’s rotation and coastlines shaping the flow. Temperature and salinity affect density and contribute to overturning, while mixing connects different depths. Surface gyres and deep circulation are related but cannot be explained by temperature alone.

teacher.script:
Select North Atlantic and identify its western and eastern boundaries. Follow the arrows and name Gulf Stream and Canary Current.

Compare South Atlantic and explain the reversed sense of rotation. Locate all five subtropical gyres.
pitfalls: Distinguish wind-driven surface gyres from the deeper overturning circulation.
Explain that the Gulf Stream transports heat as part of a wider ocean–atmosphere system.
Consider atmospheric circulation and maritime exposure as well as ocean currents when discussing the United Kingdom’s climate.

labs.title: Thermohaline conveyor
labs.hook: Seawater density depends on temperature and salinity.
labs.objective: Explain how cooling and changes in salinity affect seawater density, then relate sinking and rising water to ocean overturning.

steps.title: Observe
steps.body: Trace the upper limb, deep return and upwelling in the section. Name winds and mixing as well as buoyancy.

steps.title: Tinker
steps.body: Open Density experiment and compare parcel density with the reference. Start at Process 0: the parcel is at mid-depth. At 4 °C and 35 g/kg, play to observe descent.

steps.title: Explain
steps.body: Why can cooling and adding freshwater have opposing effects on whether a parcel of seawater sinks?

steps.title: Check
steps.body: Choose an answer and explain your reasoning. Each question includes feedback.

questions.explain: Cooling generally increases seawater density, while adding salt also makes seawater denser. These temperature and salinity effects help determine whether surface water can sink beneath surrounding water.

Strong cooling at high latitudes can make surface seawater dense enough to sink, especially where salinity is high. Sea-ice formation can further increase the salinity of nearby seawater by rejecting salt.

choices: A slow global density circulation — simplified here
questions.explain: The conveyor image links regions of sinking, deep transport and return towards the surface. Actual overturning follows many pathways and also depends on winds and mixing, rather than a single continuous belt.

choices: Always switches the conveyor off next Tuesday
Can change density and therefore sinking; it is a caution, not a countdown
Turns the Gulf Stream into a river
questions.explain: Freshwater lowers surface salinity and usually lowers density, which can strengthen stratification and inhibit deep mixing. The overall circulation response also depends on temperature, winds and where the freshwater enters.

why: Seawater density depends on temperature and salinity. Cooling and salinity changes can contribute to deep-water formation, connecting surface waters with slower circulation through the ocean interior.
Open Density experiment and compare parcel density with the reference. Start at Process 0: the parcel is at mid-depth. At 4 °C and 35 g/kg, play to observe descent.
The circulation combines several mechanisms, including winds and mixing; it is not a single conveyor driven only by temperature and salinity.

glossary.def: Relating to seawater density differences caused by temperature and salinity. These contribute to ocean overturning alongside wind forcing and mixing.
Mass divided by volume, measured in kg m⁻³. In most ocean conditions, cooling or increasing salinity makes seawater denser.
North Atlantic Deep Water: a group of deep water masses formed through cooling, mixing and sinking in the North Atlantic and neighbouring seas.

The sinking of sufficiently dense surface seawater into deeper parts of the ocean. Cooling and increased salinity can contribute, especially at high latitudes. It is one part of a complex overturning circulation that also involves mixing and upwelling.
The movement of deeper water towards the surface, often driven by winds that move surface water away or by large-scale ocean circulation.
A simplified description of interconnected deep and surface ocean circulation. Real flow involves branching currents, mixing, winds and density differences.

The concentration of dissolved salts in water. Evaporation and sea-ice formation can raise seawater salinity, while rainfall, river inflow and melting ice can lower it. Salinity and temperature together strongly influence seawater density.

misconception.claim: The ocean conveyor is one continuous pipe carrying water along a fixed route.
misconception.truth: The conveyor image simplifies a network of branching currents, mixing and exchanges between depths. Temperature and salinity influence density, while winds and mixing also help drive circulation. A parcel can follow many routes and take a range of times to move between ocean regions.

misconceptions.claim: The ocean conveyor is one continuous pipe carrying water along a fixed route.
misconceptions.truth: The conveyor image simplifies a network of branching currents, mixing and exchanges between depths. Temperature and salinity influence density, while winds and mixing also help drive circulation. A parcel can follow many routes and take a range of times to move between ocean regions.

teacher.script:
Trace the upper limb, deep return and upwelling in the section. Name winds and mixing as well as buoyancy.

Open Density experiment and compare parcel density with the reference. Start at Process 0: the parcel is at mid-depth. At 4 °C and 35 g/kg, play to observe descent.
pitfalls: Treat the conveyor image as a simplified representation of interconnected circulation rather than a single enclosed pipe.
Connect deep-water formation with seawater density and conditions at high latitudes.
Distinguish the timescales and uncertainties of real circulation change from dramatic fictional accounts.

modelNotes: The 6000 km section is 4 km deep; the usual view enlarges depth 500 times.
Reference water is 10 °C, 35 g/kg and 1027 kg/m³.
A disclosed linear approximation uses thermal expansion 0.0002 per °C and saline contraction 0.00076 per g/kg at a common reference pressure.
This is not the TEOS-10 equation of state; real coefficients and compressibility vary.
Compare 4 °C at 35 g/kg with the same temperature at 32 g/kg.

labs.title: Carbon cycle
labs.hook: Carbon moves among the atmosphere, organisms, soils, ocean and rocks.
labs.objective: Trace carbon between fast and slow stores, and explain how burning fossil fuels transfers carbon into the atmosphere.

steps.title: Observe
steps.body: Identify the five carbon stores and read their starting amounts. Close the fossil-fuel tap and play; distinguish balanced exchange from no exchange.

steps.title: Tinker
steps.body: Choose Photosynthesis and Respiration separately. Open the tap, scrub towards 100 model years, and compare source loss with total emitted carbon.

steps.title: Explain
steps.body: Explain how balanced exchanges can continue without changing a store, and how fossil-fuel burning disrupts that balance.

steps.title: Check
steps.body: Choose an answer and explain your reasoning. Each question includes feedback.

choices: A slow geologic store we tap into the fast cycle
questions.explain: Fossil fuels contain carbon stored in geological deposits over long timescales. Extraction and burning transfer that carbon rapidly into the atmosphere and other active stores.

choices: Does not talk to the air
questions.explain: Carbon dioxide can dissolve into seawater and can also leave it for the atmosphere. The direction and rate of exchange depend on the conditions on both sides of the sea surface.

Chemical weathering transfers dissolved material from rocks towards rivers and the ocean. Silicate weathering and subsequent carbonate burial participate in carbon transfers over geological timescales.

choices: Moves carbon from a slow geologic store into the atmosphere
questions.explain: Combustion combines carbon in the fuel with oxygen, releasing carbon dioxide. The carbon atoms are transferred from the fuel store into the atmosphere rather than being newly created.

why: Carbon moves among the atmosphere, organisms, soils, ocean and rocks. Photosynthesis, respiration and other transfers connect stores that operate on very different timescales.
Choose Photosynthesis and Respiration separately. Open the tap, scrub towards 100 model years, and compare source loss with total emitted carbon.
The budget tracks selected stores and transfers; compare its assumptions before interpreting it as a description of the entire global carbon cycle.

glossary.def: A quantity of material or energy held within part of a system, such as water in a lake or carbon in vegetation. Inputs and outputs change the amount stored. A store is an amount; a flux is a transfer rate.
A rate of transfer of a quantity such as water, carbon or energy; some uses express that rate per unit area.
The use of light energy to build organic molecules from carbon dioxide and water. Oxygen-producing photosynthesis transfers carbon into living matter.
Processes that release energy from organic matter. Aerobic respiration consumes oxygen and releases carbon dioxide and water.
Physical breakdown or chemical alteration of rock at or near Earth's surface, without transporting the material away. Chemical weathering also participates in the carbon cycle.
Coal, oil or natural gas formed from ancient organic material. Burning it transfers carbon from long-term geological stores to the atmosphere.
Carbon exchanges among the atmosphere, living organisms, soils and upper ocean over relatively short timescales, from days to centuries.
Carbon transfer through rocks, sediments and the deep Earth, involving weathering, burial, metamorphism and volcanism over geological timescales.

misconception.claim: Carbon released by burning fossil fuels is immediately removed by the natural carbon cycle.
misconception.truth: Burning fossil fuels transfers carbon from long-term geological stores into the atmosphere. Land and oceans absorb some of it, but uptake does not instantly match all emissions. Atmospheric carbon increases when inputs exceed removals, and different stores exchange carbon over very different timescales.

misconceptions.claim: Carbon released by burning fossil fuels is immediately removed by the natural carbon cycle.
misconceptions.truth: Burning fossil fuels transfers carbon from long-term geological stores into the atmosphere. Land and oceans absorb some of it, but uptake does not instantly match all emissions. Atmospheric carbon increases when inputs exceed removals, and different stores exchange carbon over very different timescales.

teacher.script:
Identify the five carbon stores and read their starting amounts. Close the fossil-fuel tap and play; distinguish balanced exchange from no exchange.

Choose Photosynthesis and Respiration separately. Open the tap, scrub towards 100 model years, and compare source loss with total emitted carbon.
pitfalls: Keep the carbon stores visible while explaining how each transfer changes their contents.
Explain that combustion moves existing carbon between stores rather than creating new carbon atoms.
Use the model’s stated quantities when checking conservation, and distinguish carbon mass from carbon dioxide mass.

sources.label: IPCC FAQ as school context — no invented stats

modelNotes: Starting stores are 600, 1200, 3000, 6000 and 1200 Pg C respectively.
One petagram of carbon is 10¹² kg of carbon, not of CO₂.
At the starting state, photosynthesis and respiration each transfer 60 Pg C/year, air–ocean exchange 40 in each direction, and the weathering–burial–degassing loop 0.2 on each leg.
The fossil-fuel tap adds 0–10 Pg C/year to air for up to 100 model years.
With it open, fossil carbon falls and the fast stores change while total carbon remains 12000 Pg C.

labs.title: ENSO and the Walker cell
labs.hook: Across the tropical Pacific, trade winds, warm surface water and the thermocline interact.
labs.objective: Compare normal Pacific conditions with El Niño and La Niña, and explain how changes in winds and ocean temperature affect rainfall.

steps.title: Observe
steps.body: Start at ENSO 0 and identify west, east and the thermocline. Trace rising air in the west and surface trades towards it.

steps.title: Tinker
steps.body: Move to El Niño and compare eastern temperature and thermocline depth. Compare La Niña and explain the stronger contrast.

steps.title: Explain
steps.body: How does a change in the trade winds affect Pacific surface temperatures and the location of rising air?

steps.title: Check
steps.body: Choose an answer and explain your reasoning. Each question includes feedback.

questions.explain: Under typical neutral conditions, air rises over the warmer western tropical Pacific and descends farther east. Surface trade winds and an upper-level return flow form the broad east–west Walker circulation.

choices: Shifts east in the tropical Pacific
questions.explain: During El Niño, weakened trade winds reduce the normal westward accumulation of warm surface water. The central and eastern equatorial Pacific warm, and the pattern of convection shifts eastwards.

choices: May bias odds; it does not write the month in advance
questions.explain: ENSO can alter large-scale atmospheric circulation and change the probabilities of some seasonal weather patterns. Local UK weather also depends on other influences, so an ENSO phase cannot determine a particular month's conditions.

questions.prompt: La Niña in this lab is…
choices: The opposite extra: cooler east Pacific, stronger Walker-like pattern
questions.explain: La Niña is associated with cooler-than-average central and eastern equatorial Pacific surface water and often stronger trade winds. These changes strengthen aspects of the usual east–west tropical Pacific contrast.

why: Across the tropical Pacific, trade winds, warm surface water and the thermocline interact. El Niño and La Niña describe departures from the usual coupled ocean–atmosphere pattern.
Move to El Niño and compare eastern temperature and thermocline depth. Compare La Niña and explain the stronger contrast.
The selected states illustrate these relationships; their effects on weather vary between events and places.

glossary.def: A simplified east–west tropical Pacific circulation, with rising air over warmer water and sinking air over cooler water. Its near-surface branch is linked to the trade winds. Changes in this circulation are part of ENSO.

The El Niño–Southern Oscillation is a coupled pattern of ocean and atmospheric variability in the tropical Pacific. Its warm and cool phases alter sea-surface temperature, trade winds and rainfall. These phases influence weather probabilities rather than prescribing every local event.
The warm phase of ENSO, marked by unusually warm sea-surface temperatures in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific and coupled atmospheric changes.
The cool phase of ENSO, with unusually cool central and eastern equatorial Pacific surface waters and associated changes in tropical winds and rainfall.
A region of unusually warm tropical surface water. In the Pacific, its extent and position change with winds and ENSO.
A statistical relationship between climate or weather variations in distant regions, such as the influence of ENSO on rainfall probabilities.
The movement of deeper water towards the surface, often driven by winds that move surface water away or by large-scale ocean circulation.

misconception.claim: El Niño causes the same weather in every affected place during every event.
misconception.truth: ENSO changes tropical Pacific ocean and atmospheric conditions, influencing weather probabilities in many regions. The response depends on season, event strength and other climate conditions. A regional tendency towards wetter or drier weather is not a guarantee for every location, day or event.

misconceptions.claim: El Niño causes the same weather in every affected place during every event.
misconceptions.truth: ENSO changes tropical Pacific ocean and atmospheric conditions, influencing weather probabilities in many regions. The response depends on season, event strength and other climate conditions. A regional tendency towards wetter or drier weather is not a guarantee for every location, day or event.

teacher.script:
Start at ENSO 0 and identify west, east and the thermocline. Trace rising air in the west and surface trades towards it.

Move to El Niño and compare eastern temperature and thermocline depth. Compare La Niña and explain the stronger contrast.
pitfalls: Locate the changing trade winds, warm water and rising air in the tropical Pacific before discussing effects elsewhere.
Describe ENSO as a pattern that changes the likelihood of regional conditions rather than a forecast for a specific day.
Ask students to explain the ocean–atmosphere interaction before connecting the model with a distant weather event.

labs.title: Landform types
labs.hook: Elevation, relief, slope and shape describe different properties of terrain.
labs.objective: Compare the elevation and shape of mountains, hills, plateaus, plains and basins using a shared scale.

steps.title: Observe
steps.body: Compare Mountain with Plain at the common scale. Distinguish elevation from local relief.

steps.title: Tinker
steps.body: Replace Plain with Plateau and explain its high flat surface. Compare Hill and Basin, then rotate both.

steps.title: Explain
steps.body: Why is elevation alone insufficient to distinguish a plateau, a mountain and a plain?

steps.title: Check
steps.body: Choose an answer and explain your reasoning. Each question includes feedback.

choices: An elevated area with a relatively flat top
questions.explain: A plateau is elevated relative to surrounding terrain but retains a broad, comparatively level surface. Rivers may dissect it into valleys and canyons without removing its overall plateau setting.

choices: A depression; drainage often inward or along the floor
questions.explain: A basin is a lower area relative to the land around it. Water may converge towards its floor, although not every basin is completely enclosed or internally drained.

questions.prompt: A mountain vs a hill is mainly…
choices: Relief, slope and local height — a continuum, not a law
questions.explain: Mountains and hills differ in relative height, slope and relief, but those properties vary continuously. No single height threshold is used consistently in every country and context.

questions.prompt: The Grand Canyon is best described as…
choices: A canyon cut into a plateau
questions.explain: The Colorado River and its tributaries incised the elevated Colorado Plateau. The canyon is therefore a deeply cut valley within a plateau, rather than a glacial trough or an isolated mountain.

why: Elevation, relief, slope and shape describe different properties of terrain. A plateau can stand high above sea level while remaining relatively flat, and a basin is defined by its lower position relative to nearby land.
Replace Plain with Plateau and explain its high flat surface. Compare Hill and Basin, then rotate both.
The five terrain samples use a shared scale for comparison; shape alone does not establish the process or rock type that formed a landscape.

glossary.def: A landform with substantial elevation and relief relative to its surroundings. There is no single globally accepted height separating mountains from hills.

An area of raised ground with relief above its surroundings, generally smaller than a mountain. Shape and local context matter: there is no universal height that separates the two. Contours can show its summit, slopes and relative height.

An extensive area of elevated, relatively level ground. Rivers can dissect it into deep valleys and canyons while remnants of the high surface remain. A plateau describes broad relief rather than a particular rock type.

A broad area of relatively low relief, often but not always at low elevation. Plains can form by deposition, erosion or other processes. Flatness alone does not identify how a particular plain developed.
A low area surrounded by higher ground. A drainage basin is the land area that sends water to a particular river, lake or other outlet.
The variation in elevation within an area, often expressed as the difference between its highest and lowest points.

A deep valley with steep sides, commonly cut by a river into elevated rock. The surrounding plateau and the canyon are different landforms. Rock resistance, uplift and changing base level all influence how the valley develops.

misconception.claim: A landform’s shape tells us which single process created it.
misconception.truth: A landscape can record several processes acting at different times. A river may occupy a valley widened by ice, while rock structure influences both erosion and slope failure. Shape provides clues, but interpreting the history also needs evidence such as sediments, rock relationships and chronology.

misconceptions.claim: A landform’s shape tells us which single process created it.
misconceptions.truth: A landscape can record several processes acting at different times. A river may occupy a valley widened by ice, while rock structure influences both erosion and slope failure. Shape provides clues, but interpreting the history also needs evidence such as sediments, rock relationships and chronology.

teacher.script:
Compare Mountain with Plain at the common scale. Distinguish elevation from local relief.

Replace Plain with Plateau and explain its high flat surface. Compare Hill and Basin, then rotate both.
pitfalls: Use landform categories to organise observations without treating them as universal rules with sharp boundaries.
Distinguish a canyon cut into a landscape from a mountain range raised by tectonic processes.
Explain that the distinction between a hill and a mountain does not have one universally accepted height threshold.

labs.title: River erosion
labs.hook: Flowing water can detach and transport material from a river’s bed and banks.
labs.objective: Explain how river erosion forms waterfalls, gorges and potholes, and distinguish the retreat of a waterfall from the direction of flow.

steps.title: Observe
steps.body: Follow water downstream, then identify the lip and plunge pool.

steps.title: Tinker
steps.body: Change Retreat to move the lip upstream; select Pothole or V-shaped valley.

steps.title: Explain
steps.body: Explain why a waterfall can retreat upstream while the water continues to flow downstream.

steps.title: Check
steps.body: Choose an answer and explain your reasoning. Each question includes feedback.

choices: A gorge upstream of the old fall
questions.explain: Erosion and collapse can make a waterfall retreat upstream. The narrow, steep-sided valley left between its former and current positions forms a gorge.

choices: Pebbles swirling and abrading the bed
questions.explain: Eddying water can trap stones and sand in a bedrock hollow and repeatedly move them against its sides. This abrasion deepens and widens a river pothole.

A river cutting down into its bed creates a narrow valley floor while weathering and slope processes lower the sides. Together these processes commonly produce a V-shaped cross-section in upland valleys.

questions.prompt: The Grand Canyon formed mainly by…
questions.explain: The Colorado River cut down through rock layers as the regional landscape evolved and the plateau rose. The exposed rocks are much older than the canyon carved through them.

why: Flowing water can detach and transport material from a river’s bed and banks. Hydraulic action and abrasion contribute to erosion, while differences in rock resistance can influence the resulting forms.
Change Retreat to move the lip upstream; select Pothole or V-shaped valley.
The selected stages explain mechanisms and changing form; they do not assign a measured erosion rate to a real river.

glossary.def: An abrupt steepening in a river’s long profile, also written knickpoint. A waterfall is one example. Resistant rock, uplift or a change in base level can produce one, and erosion may cause it to migrate upstream.

A narrow, steep-sided valley. One way it can develop is through the retreat of a waterfall, leaving a deeply cut channel downstream. The surrounding rock and the river’s erosive history control its form.

A deep hollow at the foot of a waterfall, enlarged by turbulent water and sediment striking the bed. Undercutting and collapse may contribute to waterfall retreat. The pool’s form also depends on rock structure, discharge and sediment supply.

A rounded hollow eroded into a rocky riverbed by turbulent water and circulating sediment. Trapped stones may assist abrasion as water swirls. It differs from a large plunge pool formed directly beneath a waterfall.

A valley with a broadly V-shaped cross-section, commonly developed where river downcutting and slope processes work together. Its form depends on rock, climate and erosion history. A V shape is evidence to interpret, not proof of one process acting alone.

Erosion caused by the force of moving water, including pressure fluctuations and water or trapped air acting within cracks. It can loosen material from a riverbank or coast. Abrasion adds the separate effect of sediment striking those surfaces.

The wearing away of rock by sediment carried against it by water, wind or ice. Look for scratches, polished surfaces or potholes. Unlike attrition, abrasion describes damage to the surface being struck, rather than collisions between transported particles.

The breakdown and rounding of transported particles as they collide with one another. Pebbles may become smaller and smoother during repeated transport. This differs from abrasion, in which those particles wear away the bed, bank or another fixed surface.

misconception.claim: Weathering and river erosion describe the same process.
misconception.truth: Weathering breaks down or alters rock in place, while erosion wears away and removes material. A river can exploit rock weakened by weathering and use transported sediment to abrade its bed. The processes can work together without being interchangeable.

misconceptions.claim: Weathering and river erosion describe the same process.
misconceptions.truth: Weathering breaks down or alters rock in place, while erosion wears away and removes material. A river can exploit rock weakened by weathering and use transported sediment to abrade its bed. The processes can work together without being interchangeable.

teacher.script:
Follow water downstream, then identify the lip and plunge pool.

Change Retreat to move the lip upstream; select Pothole or V-shaped valley.
pitfalls: Compare valley shapes and rock conditions rather than describing every river valley as a canyon.
Explain how erosion and collapse can cause a waterfall to retreat upstream.
Distinguish the age of the rocks from the time over which the river excavated the valley.

modelNotes: Change Retreat to move the lip through a prescribed 25 m sequence; the falling water and plunge pool follow the new lip.
The waterfall and valley view enlarges vertical relief 1.5 times; Physical scale restores common distances.

labs.title: River deposition
labs.hook: Sediment is deposited when transport conditions no longer keep it moving.
labs.objective: Explain where rivers deposit sediment and compare the formation of point bars, natural levees and deltas.

steps.title: Observe
steps.body: Locate the inner bank and point bar.

steps.title: Tinker
steps.body: Compare overbank flow and a delta; change the separate settling experiment.

steps.title: Explain
steps.body: Why can a river erode its outer bank while depositing sediment on the inner bank?

steps.title: Check
steps.body: Choose an answer and explain your reasoning. Each question includes feedback.

choices: Deposition on the inner bend of a meander
questions.explain: Flow around a meander transports sediment towards the inner bend, where near-bank velocities and transport capacity are often lower. Deposition there builds a point bar and its gently sloping surface.

choices: Floodwater leaves the channel and dumps coarse load on the banks
questions.explain: When floodwater leaves the channel, it slows and deposits much of its coarser suspended sediment near the banks. Repeated floods can build raised natural levées alongside the river.

questions.prompt: Many UK rivers end in estuaries because…
choices: Tidal range and a drowned coast can outpace delta building
questions.explain: Strong tidal exchange can redistribute river sediment, while rising relative sea level can drown a river valley. These conditions favour an estuary where sediment supply is insufficient to build a delta outward.

questions.prompt: The outer bank of a meander is mainly a site of…
questions.explain: Faster flow and greater shear stress commonly occur near a meander's outer bank. Undercutting and bank collapse then help the bend migrate outward.

why: Sediment is deposited when transport conditions no longer keep it moving. Inner bends, floodplains and river mouths create different settings for sorting and storing sediment.
Compare overbank flow and a delta; change the separate settling experiment.
The separate settling experiment describes small quartz spheres in still water; river turbulence and flocculation can change their behaviour.

glossary.def: The gently sloping inner bank of a river bend, where sediment tends to accumulate as a point bar. It contrasts with the steeper outer cut bank. Both develop as the bend migrates and its flow redistributes sediment.

The eroding outer bank of a river bend, where the faster part of the flow commonly approaches the bank. A steep face or exposed roots can reveal active erosion. Deposition often occurs on a point bar across the channel.
A raised bank beside a river, either built naturally by overbank sediment deposition or constructed to reduce flooding. Also written levee.
Relatively flat land beside a river that is shaped by channel migration and flood deposition and may be inundated when the river overflows.
A body of sediment built where a river enters a sea or lake and deposits enough material to accumulate. Distributary channels often cross its surface.
A partly enclosed coastal water body where freshwater meets and mixes with seawater, influenced by tides.

A secondary, spiral-like circulation within a river bend, superimposed on the downstream current. Near-bed movement helps transfer sediment towards the inner bank, while strong flow near the outer bank promotes erosion. The pattern varies with channel shape and discharge.

misconception.claim: A river deposits all its sediment as soon as the water slows down.
misconception.truth: Deposition depends on the ability of the flow to keep particular particles moving. Coarser material often settles or stops first as transport capacity falls, while finer particles may remain suspended farther downstream. Sediment size, turbulence, water depth and incoming supply all affect the result.

misconceptions.claim: A river deposits all its sediment as soon as the water slows down.
misconceptions.truth: Deposition depends on the ability of the flow to keep particular particles moving. Coarser material often settles or stops first as transport capacity falls, while finer particles may remain suspended farther downstream. Sediment size, turbulence, water depth and incoming supply all affect the result.

teacher.script:
Locate the inner bank and point bar.

Compare overbank flow and a delta; change the separate settling experiment.
pitfalls: Distinguish sediment accumulation in a delta from processes operating in a tidal estuary.
Locate inner-bank deposition and outer-bank erosion correctly when interpreting a meander.
Explain that levees can form naturally during floods as well as being built or enlarged by people.

modelNotes: A separate Stokes calculation uses isolated 10–50 μm quartz spheres, still fresh water at 20 °C, density 998 kg/m³ and dynamic viscosity 1.002 mPa·s.
It estimates terminal settling speed and the distance travelled at 0.1 m/s through 2 m depth.

labs.title: River capture
labs.hook: Headward erosion can extend one river into a neighbouring basin and divert its headwaters.
labs.objective: Explain how headward erosion can divert a river’s headwaters and identify evidence left in the old channel.

steps.title: Observe
steps.body: Identify the two separate water routes and their outlets.

steps.title: Tinker
steps.body: Step towards the divide and then After capture; play the changed water route.

steps.title: Explain
steps.body: How does diverting the headwaters affect the captured river and the abandoned part of its old valley?

steps.title: Check
steps.body: Choose an answer and explain your reasoning. Each question includes feedback.

choices: A sharp bend where the captured stream now turns into the pirate
questions.explain: When a stream is diverted into a neighbouring drainage system, it may turn sharply at the capture point. That abrupt change in course can form an elbow of capture.

choices: Loses its headwaters and often shrinks
questions.explain: A beheaded stream loses part of its upstream drainage area and therefore often loses discharge. The remaining stream may be too small to account for the size of its inherited valley.

choices: Both rivers sit at the same height forever
One has a steeper gradient or weaker rock and cuts back faster
questions.explain: A stream with a greater erosive advantage can extend its headwaters back towards a neighbouring basin. If it breaches the divide, it may divert the neighbouring headwaters into its own channel.

questions.prompt: What does the Mississippi Old River Control Structure illustrate?
choices: Engineering can limit diversion towards the Atchafalaya; this is flow-diversion control, not the headward-erosion mechanism shown here.
questions.explain: The Old River Control Structure regulates how Mississippi flow divides towards the Atchafalaya. This is an example of managing potential river diversion, which differs from the headward erosion shown in the capture model.

why: Headward erosion can extend one river into a neighbouring basin and divert its headwaters. The new route may leave an elbow of capture and a former valley carrying a much smaller stream.
Step towards the divide and then After capture; play the changed water route.
The chosen stages show one capture mechanism; their spacing does not represent an erosion rate or dated sequence.

glossary.def: A sharp bend marking where one drainage system has diverted water from another. It can help reconstruct river capture when combined with a wind gap or underfit valley. A sharp bend alone is not enough to prove capture.
A stream whose former headwaters have been diverted into another drainage system by river capture.

The stream that gains water by capturing the headwaters of another drainage system. It may extend its valley by headward erosion. The term describes a changed drainage connection, not a different type of flowing water.

A valley crossing a drainage divide that no longer contains the stream that cut it. It can be evidence of river capture or another drainage change. Compare its shape with neighbouring valleys and the present stream network.

The extension of a valley or channel back towards its source by erosion. Over time it can shift a drainage divide and help one river capture another’s headwaters. It describes growth upstream, not water flowing uphill.
In UK geography, the drainage divide separating basins. In US usage, watershed commonly means the entire drainage basin; check the context.
A stream smaller than the valley it occupies, sometimes following river capture or the loss of former glacial meltwater discharge.

misconception.claim: A drainage divide is permanent, so one river cannot gain another river’s headwaters.
misconception.truth: Erosion, tectonic change or other landscape adjustment can shift a divide and divert flow into a neighbouring basin. The capturing river gains drainage area while the former channel may carry a smaller stream. Landforms such as wind gaps can help reconstruct the change.

misconceptions.claim: A drainage divide is permanent, so one river cannot gain another river’s headwaters.
misconceptions.truth: Erosion, tectonic change or other landscape adjustment can shift a divide and divert flow into a neighbouring basin. The capturing river gains drainage area while the former channel may carry a smaller stream. Landforms such as wind gaps can help reconstruct the change.

teacher.script:
Identify the two separate water routes and their outlets.

Step towards the divide and then After capture; play the changed water route.
pitfalls: Present river capture as the result of evolving drainage and erosion rather than an instantaneous change without a cause.
Explain how a drainage divide can migrate as neighbouring river systems erode their headwaters.
Use features such as a wind gap to discuss the evidence for an earlier drainage pattern.

labs.title: Coasts
labs.hook: Waves erode rock, transport sediment and deposit it along the coast.
labs.objective: Explain how coastal erosion forms caves, arches and stacks, and how longshore drift and groynes change the movement of beach sediment.

steps.title: Observe
steps.body: Inspect the cave back wall, then compare the open arch.

steps.title: Tinker
steps.body: Select Beach transport and Groyne, or compare the attached spit.

steps.title: Explain
steps.body: How can retaining sediment at one groyne affect beaches farther along the coast?

steps.title: Check
steps.body: Choose an answer and explain your reasoning. Each question includes feedback.

choices: Along the beach in the direction of the angled swash
questions.explain: Waves approaching at an angle carry sediment diagonally up the beach in the swash. Backwash returns more directly downslope, producing a net movement along the coast over repeated waves.

choices: An isolated pillar after an arch collapses
questions.explain: Wave erosion can enlarge a cave into an arch through a headland. When the arch roof collapses, an isolated pillar remains as a stack.

choices: Trap sediment up-drift and can starve down-drift
questions.explain: Groynes interrupt sediment transported along the beach and encourage accumulation on their up-drift side. Unless sediment is supplied from elsewhere, less may reach the coast down-drift.

questions.prompt: How should a sea wall be assessed within a whole-coast budget?
choices: Local protection can alter neighbouring processes; effects depend on the setting and design.
questions.explain: A sea wall protects a particular frontage but can alter wave reflection, local scour and sediment exchanges. Its effects should therefore be assessed within the connected coastal sediment system.

why: Waves erode rock, transport sediment and deposit it along the coast. The resulting landforms depend on rock structure, wave direction, sediment supply and the balance of material entering and leaving a coastal section.
Select Beach transport and Groyne, or compare the attached spit.
The scene demonstrates selected coastal processes; a real shoreline’s response also depends on its wider sediment budget.

glossary.def: A classroom description of waves that tend to build a beach because swash carries more sediment landward than backwash removes. Whether a beach actually grows also depends on sediment supply, slope and changing conditions over the whole wave cycle.
A teaching description for waves that tend to remove sediment from a beach, with strong backwash relative to swash. Net change also depends on sediment and wave conditions.

The net movement of beach sediment along a coast as oblique waves drive swash up the beach and gravity returns backwash downslope. Direction depends on wave approach. Structures that interrupt the supply can change beaches farther along the coast.
An elongated deposit of sand or shingle attached to land at one end and extending into water, commonly built by longshore sediment transport.
An isolated pillar of coastal rock left by erosion and cliff retreat, sometimes after the collapse of a sea arch. Old Harry is chalk; Durdle Door is an arch in limestone.

The low remnant of an eroded sea stack, often visible only at low tide. Wave action and weathering reduce the isolated rock over time. The cave–arch–stack–stump sequence is useful, although real coasts can follow more complicated histories.

A structure extending across a beach to interrupt longshore sediment movement. Sand may build up on its up-drift side while the down-drift beach receives less. Its effects should be considered within the wider coastal sediment budget.

An accounting of sediment entering, leaving and being stored within a defined area. A beach can erode when losses exceed supply, even if deposition occurs briefly. State the boundaries and time period before comparing inputs and outputs.

misconception.claim: Groynes create new beach sediment without affecting nearby coasts.
misconception.truth: Groynes interrupt alongshore sediment movement and can retain material on one side. They redistribute an existing supply rather than create it, potentially reducing delivery farther along the coast. Their effects therefore need to be considered within the wider sediment budget.

misconceptions.claim: Groynes create new beach sediment without affecting nearby coasts.
misconceptions.truth: Groynes interrupt alongshore sediment movement and can retain material on one side. They redistribute an existing supply rather than create it, potentially reducing delivery farther along the coast. Their effects therefore need to be considered within the wider sediment budget.

teacher.script:
Inspect the cave back wall, then compare the open arch.

Select Beach transport and Groyne, or compare the attached spit.
pitfalls: Consider sediment inputs and outputs when explaining how a coastal landform changes.
Distinguish a stack of resistant rock from a spit built by sediment deposition.
Ask how a sea wall or other defence affects neighbouring sections of coast rather than judging only the protected site.

modelNotes: The rock has real openings and uses a common 10 m geometric scale.

labs.title: Glacial landforms
labs.hook: Glacier ice flows downslope under gravity, even when its margin is retreating.
labs.objective: Explain how moving ice shapes a valley, and distinguish the direction of ice flow from the advance or retreat of its margin.

steps.title: Observe
steps.body: Trace down-valley ice flow from the accumulation area.

steps.title: Tinker
steps.body: Change Ice extent, then Play. Ice still flows down-valley during retreat.

steps.title: Explain
steps.body: Explain how a glacier’s margin can retreat even while its ice continues to flow down the valley.

steps.title: Check
steps.body: Choose an answer and explain your reasoning. Each question includes feedback.

choices: A knife ridge between two cirques
questions.explain: Glaciers eroding neighbouring cirques can steepen the valley walls on both sides of an intervening ridge. The narrow ridge left between them is an arête.

choices: Three or more cirques eating a peak
questions.explain: When several cirques erode back towards the same summit, they steepen its sides from different directions. The remaining sharply pointed summit is a horn or pyramidal peak.

questions.prompt: A U-shaped trough vs a V…
choices: Ice overdeepens a wide floor; rivers cut a V
questions.explain: A valley glacier abrades and plucks both the floor and sides of a pre-existing valley, widening and deepening it. A river more commonly concentrates erosion within a narrower channel, helping produce a V-shaped profile.

choices: A river canyon like the Grand Canyon
questions.explain: Glaciers repeatedly enlarged an earlier river valley in Yosemite's granitic bedrock. Their erosion produced the broad floor and steep walls characteristic of its glacial trough.

why: Glacier ice flows downslope under gravity, even when its margin is retreating. Erosion by ice and carried debris can deepen valleys and shape cirques, arêtes and horns.
Change Ice extent, then Play. Ice still flows down-valley during retreat.
Changing ice extent compares margin positions; it does not reverse ice flow or calculate the glacier’s mass balance.

glossary.def: A bowl-shaped hollow with steep sides at the head of a glacial valley, enlarged by ice erosion and weathering. A lake, called a tarn, may occupy it after the ice retreats.
A narrow, sharp ridge formed where glaciers erode adjoining valleys or cirques. Striding Edge in the Lake District is an example.
A sharp pyramidal mountain peak formed by erosion from glaciers on several sides; the Matterhorn is a well-known example.

A valley with a broad floor and steep sides produced or enlarged by glacial erosion. It contrasts with the narrower V-shaped cross-section often associated with river incision. Later rivers and slope processes continue modifying the glacial valley.
An accumulation of debris transported or deposited by a glacier, including lateral, medial, terminal and ground moraines.

Unsorted sediment deposited directly by glacier ice, often containing a mixture from clay to boulders. Its poor sorting distinguishes it from many meltwater deposits reworked by flowing water. Till can form several types of glacial landform.

A tributary valley whose floor lies above the floor of the main glacial trough. The larger glacier commonly erodes more deeply than its tributary. After ice retreat, a waterfall may connect the two valley levels.
An elongated hill streamlined beneath moving ice, commonly made of glacial sediment and sometimes containing bedrock. Its long axis usually follows former ice flow.

misconception.claim: A retreating glacier must be flowing uphill.
misconception.truth: Glacier ice generally moves downslope under gravity even when its terminus retreats. The front moves back when local ice loss exceeds the supply of ice moving towards it. Ice velocity and the change in the terminus position describe different aspects of glacier behaviour.

misconceptions.claim: A retreating glacier must be flowing uphill.
misconceptions.truth: Glacier ice generally moves downslope under gravity even when its terminus retreats. The front moves back when local ice loss exceeds the supply of ice moving towards it. Ice velocity and the change in the terminus position describe different aspects of glacier behaviour.

teacher.script:
Trace down-valley ice flow from the accumulation area.

Change Ice extent, then Play. Ice still flows down-valley during retreat.
pitfalls: Compare Yosemite’s glacial trough with a predominantly river-cut canyon to distinguish the processes shaping them.
Explain that glaciers can occur in high mountains as well as polar regions.
Consider the thickness and movement of the ice when explaining erosion and deposition.

sources.label: NPS ice flow and glacier margin change

modelNotes: Default relief is enlarged 1.5 times; Physical scale restores a common kilometre scale.

labs.title: Karst
labs.hook: Water containing dissolved carbon dioxide can dissolve calcite along joints and bedding planes.
labs.objective: Explain how water dissolves limestone along joints to form surface grooves, sinkholes and underground passages.

steps.title: Observe
steps.body: Identify clints, grykes and the surface depression.

steps.title: Tinker
steps.body: Open Cutaway and follow the selected route towards the spring.

steps.title: Explain
steps.body: How do joints and slightly acidic water influence the development of limestone passages?

steps.title: Check
steps.body: Choose an answer and explain your reasoning. Each question includes feedback.

choices: Dissolved fissures between clints on a limestone pavement
questions.explain: Weakly acidic water dissolves limestone along joints, widening them into grykes. The remaining blocks between those fissures are called clints.

choices: Where a surface stream sinks underground
questions.explain: A swallow hole is an opening where surface water enters an underground drainage route. Enlarged joints and solution passages in limestone commonly provide that route.

questions.prompt: Karst clusters on carbonate rocks because…
questions.explain: Rainwater containing dissolved carbon dioxide forms weak carbonic acid, which reacts with calcium carbonate. Flow through joints gradually enlarges openings in carbonate rocks and develops karst drainage.

questions.prompt: The caves in this lab are…
questions.explain: These caves form as flowing water dissolves carbonate rock along fractures and other openings. Their origin is chemically distinct from a lava tube left by flowing molten rock.

why: Water containing dissolved carbon dioxide can dissolve calcite along joints and bedding planes. Connected openings can develop into underground drainage routes, while calcite may later precipitate where carbon dioxide escapes.
Open Cutaway and follow the selected route towards the spring.
The cutaway illustrates connected passages and the reaction; it does not calculate cave growth rates or water quality.

glossary.def: An exposed limestone surface divided into blocks called clints and solution-enlarged joints called grykes. Glacial stripping can expose the rock, after which chemical weathering enlarges fractures. The pavement records both exposure and later dissolution.

A block of limestone at the surface of a limestone pavement, separated from neighbouring blocks by enlarged joints called grykes. Rainwater containing weak carbonic acid dissolves the rock along those joints and can also carve grooves into each clint.

A deepened joint or fissure separating clints on a limestone pavement. Weakly acidic water dissolves limestone along the fracture and widens it. Plants often occupy grykes because they trap soil and offer shelter.
An opening where a surface stream enters underground drainage, usually in karst. A doline or sinkhole is a depression and need not contain a sinking stream.
Chemical weathering in which dissolved carbon dioxide forms weak carbonic acid that reacts with carbonate minerals such as calcite.

A place where water that flowed underground returns to the surface, often as a spring in karst terrain. Tracer studies can link a resurgence to a distant sinking stream. The visible outlet does not reveal the whole underground route.

A mineral deposit hanging from a cave roof, commonly formed when dripping water loses carbon dioxide and precipitates calcite. A stalagmite grows upward from the floor. Neither feature is formed by limestone simply melting.

misconception.claim: An underground drainage basin must have exactly the same boundary as the surface basin.
misconception.truth: Water in soluble rock can follow connected fractures and passages beneath a surface divide. Its underground route may therefore lead to a different outlet from the one suggested by topography. Dye tracing and other observations can help establish the actual groundwater connections.

misconceptions.claim: An underground drainage basin must have exactly the same boundary as the surface basin.
misconceptions.truth: Water in soluble rock can follow connected fractures and passages beneath a surface divide. Its underground route may therefore lead to a different outlet from the one suggested by topography. Dye tracing and other observations can help establish the actual groundwater connections.

teacher.script:
Identify clints, grykes and the surface depression.

Open Cutaway and follow the selected route towards the spring.
pitfalls: Connect solution landforms with water moving through soluble rock rather than assuming every hollow is volcanic.
Distinguish limestone solution caves from lava tubes formed during volcanic activity.
Use an appropriate soluble rock, such as limestone, when explaining the development of karst.

modelNotes: Water containing dissolved carbon dioxide can dissolve calcite: CaCO₃ + CO₂ + H₂O → Ca²⁺ + 2HCO₃⁻.
The 60 by 30 m block uses 1.3-fold vertical exaggeration unless T is selected.

labs.title: Folds and faults
labs.hook: Rock layers may bend into folds or break and move along faults.
labs.objective: Compare the rock deformation caused by compression, tension and sideways motion, using folds and faults as evidence.

steps.title: Observe
steps.body: Choose Anticline and identify the oldest bed. Compare Syncline; explain why age and shape are different criteria.

steps.title: Tinker
steps.body: Choose Normal fault and name hanging wall before playing. Reverse the sense of slip with Reverse fault, then compare lateral displacement in Strike-slip.

steps.title: Explain
steps.body: Use the movement of the hanging wall to distinguish a normal fault from a reverse fault.

steps.title: Check
steps.body: Choose an answer and explain your reasoning. Each question includes feedback.

questions.prompt: In this upright example, an anticline is…
choices: An upfold with older beds towards the core.
questions.explain: An anticline has older strata towards its core, even if later deformation overturns the fold. In the upright example, this age arrangement coincides with an upward arch.
Extension pulls the crust apart, allowing the hanging-wall block to move down relative to the footwall along a normal fault. The movement lengthens the crust across the fault system.
The San Andreas mainly accommodates horizontal movement between adjacent plate blocks. This sideways displacement makes it a strike-slip fault and a transform plate boundary.

choices: The block above the fault plane
questions.explain: The hanging wall is the rock block above an inclined fault plane, while the footwall lies below it. These names identify geometry and do not depend on which block moved upwards.

why: Rock layers may bend into folds or break and move along faults. Layer age, orientation and relative movement help distinguish structures that can look similar from one viewing angle.
Choose Normal fault and name hanging wall before playing. Reverse the sense of slip with Reverse fault, then compare lateral displacement in Strike-slip.
The deformation is prescribed to reveal structure; it does not solve rock failure or the stresses at a particular site.

glossary.def: A fold with the oldest rocks in its core. In a simple upright anticline, the layers arch upwards and dip away from the centre; overturned folds can have different geometry.
A fold with the youngest rocks in its core. In a simple upright syncline, layers dip towards the centre; erosion can leave either a ridge or valley above it.

A fault on which the hanging wall moves down relative to the footwall. It commonly forms where the crust is being extended. Determine movement from displaced layers rather than the present height of the land surface alone.

A fault on which the hanging wall moves up relative to the footwall, commonly under compression. A low-angle reverse fault is called a thrust. Displaced rock layers help identify motion even after erosion changes the surface.
Fault movement that is mainly horizontal and parallel to the fault's strike. Some strike-slip faults form plate-transform boundaries; others lie within plates.

The block above an inclined fault plane. In a normal fault it moves downward relative to the footwall, while in a reverse fault it moves upward. The names describe position relative to the plane, not present elevation.

The block of rock below an inclined fault plane. Identify it from the geometry of the plane before describing movement. In a normal fault the hanging wall moves down relative to the footwall; reverse motion is the opposite.
In structural geology, the uplift and shortening of a previously subsiding basin. A temperature inversion in meteorology is a different use of the word.

misconception.claim: The hanging wall is always the side of a fault that moves down.
misconception.truth: The hanging wall is defined by its position above an inclined fault plane. It moves down relative to the footwall in a normal fault and up in a reverse fault. Identify the plane and blocks before using their displacement to name the fault type.

misconceptions.claim: The hanging wall is always the side of a fault that moves down.
misconceptions.truth: The hanging wall is defined by its position above an inclined fault plane. It moves down relative to the footwall in a normal fault and up in a reverse fault. Identify the plane and blocks before using their displacement to name the fault type.

teacher.script:
Choose Anticline and identify the oldest bed. Compare Syncline; explain why age and shape are different criteria.

Choose Normal fault and name hanging wall before playing. Reverse the sense of slip with Reverse fault, then compare lateral displacement in Strike-slip.
pitfalls: Identify the hanging wall and footwall from their positions relative to the fault plane before describing movement.
Explain how rock can deform over geological time; a soft classroom material only helps visualise the resulting shape.
Distinguish horizontal movement along the San Andreas system from subduction at Cascadia.

modelNotes: In the faults, a 60° dipping plane separates the footwall below it from the hanging wall above.
The maximum relative fault slip is 700 m, and the readout separates that slip from its vertical throw.

labs.title: Wind landforms
labs.hook: Wind transports particles by suspension, saltation and surface creep.
labs.objective: Explain how wind erodes rock and transports sand, then identify the wind direction from the shape of a barchan dune.

steps.title: Observe
steps.body: Find the wind arrow and the dune horns pointing downwind.

steps.title: Tinker
steps.body: Compare Barchan dune with Yardang ridges; Play follows enlarged grains.

steps.title: Explain
steps.body: How do erosion and deposition produce different landforms under the action of wind?

steps.title: Check
steps.body: Choose an answer and explain your reasoning. Each question includes feedback.

questions.explain: A barchan forms under a dominant wind direction with a limited sand supply. Its thinner margins move faster than the thicker centre, extending the horns downwind.
Wind-driven abrasion and the removal of loose material can carve elongated ridges from susceptible ground. These streamlined erosional landforms are called yardangs.

choices: Loose sediment and enough wind, often sparse vegetation
questions.explain: Wind can entrain and transport sediment when exposed particles are loose and the wind is strong enough. Vegetation and soil moisture usually make that removal more difficult.

questions.prompt: The Dust Bowl’s headline process was…
choices: A barchan dune sea covering the plains
Deflation of a bare A horizon after plough and drought
questions.explain: Drought and cultivation left extensive areas of soil exposed during the Dust Bowl. Strong winds removed and transported the vulnerable topsoil, rather than simply building desert dune fields.

why: Wind transports particles by suspension, saltation and surface creep. Where sand supply and wind conditions allow accumulation, deposition builds dunes whose shapes reflect transport and local obstacles.
Compare Barchan dune with Yardang ridges; Play follows enlarged grains.
The examples show selected forms and transport directions; dune migration speed requires additional wind and sediment evidence.

glossary.def: An elongated ridge shaped by wind erosion in relatively soft material, typically aligned with the prevailing erosive wind. Abrasion and deflation carve the surrounding grooves. A yardang is an erosional landform, unlike a dune built by deposition.
A crescent-shaped dune formed where sand supply is limited and wind mainly blows from one direction. Its horns extend downwind.

The removal of loose surface particles by wind. Fine material may be carried away in suspension, leaving a coarser lag behind. Deflation removes sediment; abrasion is the wearing of surfaces by particles that the wind carries.
Transport in short hops or bounces, especially of sand grains moved by wind or flowing water.
Transport of fine sediment within moving water or air, kept aloft by turbulence rather than continuously resting on the bed or ground.

A mound of windblown sediment accumulated around a shrub or other vegetation. The plant slows nearby airflow and traps moving grains. Its shape and growth reflect the interaction between vegetation, wind and sediment supply rather than wind direction alone.

A broad region covered by wind-deposited sand and dunes, often called a sand sea. An erg needs a supply of sand and conditions that allow it to accumulate. Many deserts instead have mainly rocky or gravel surfaces.

misconception.claim: Every desert is covered by dunes.
misconception.truth: Many deserts expose bedrock, gravel or other surfaces with little loose sand. Dunes require a suitable sediment supply and wind conditions that allow accumulation. Wind can erode one area while depositing material elsewhere, so aridity alone does not determine the landform.

misconceptions.claim: Every desert is covered by dunes.
misconceptions.truth: Many deserts expose bedrock, gravel or other surfaces with little loose sand. Dunes require a suitable sediment supply and wind conditions that allow accumulation. Wind can erode one area while depositing material elsewhere, so aridity alone does not determine the landform.

teacher.script:
Find the wind arrow and the dune horns pointing downwind.

Compare Barchan dune with Yardang ridges; Play follows enlarged grains.
pitfalls: Explain that deserts can have rocky or gravel surfaces as well as areas covered by dunes.
Check that the horns of a barchan dune point downwind when students describe its shape.
Distinguish the movement of individual grains from the slower migration of an entire dune.

modelNotes: This prescribed example has a gentler stoss slope and a 32° central lee slip face at true scale.

labs.title: Rock cycle
labs.hook: Rocks can change through melting, crystallisation, weathering, deposition, burial and metamorphism.
labs.objective: Trace several possible routes through the rock cycle and explain how melting, cooling, pressure and weathering transform rock.

steps.title: Observe
steps.body: Identify three rock groups, loose sediment and magma.

steps.title: Tinker
steps.body: Choose several paths, including a solid-state and a melting path.

steps.title: Explain
steps.body: Choose a pathway that does not involve melting and explain how it transforms the original rock.

steps.title: Check
steps.body: Choose an answer and explain your reasoning. Each question includes feedback.

questions.explain: Metamorphism changes minerals or rock texture in response to conditions such as heat, pressure and fluids while the rock remains largely solid. Melting produces magma and begins a different transformation pathway.

questions.prompt: Melt becomes an igneous rock through…
questions.explain: As melt loses heat, minerals can crystallise and form an igneous rock. Very rapid cooling can instead preserve some or all of the material as volcanic glass.

questions.prompt: Which statement about the rock cycle is sound?
choices: Every rock follows the same ordered circuit.
Different paths can skip stages or repeat changes.
All sedimentary rocks have identical layers.
questions.explain: A rock can follow many paths depending on burial, uplift, weathering, heating and melting. The rock cycle describes possible transformations rather than a fixed sequence that every rock must complete.
