choices: Do not determine the outcome without composition and other conditions.
questions.explain: Temperature and pressure help constrain the possible changes, but the starting composition, fluids and duration also matter. Two rocks at the same temperature and pressure need not develop identical minerals or textures.

why: Rocks can change through melting, crystallisation, weathering, deposition, burial and metamorphism. These processes form a network of possible routes rather than a compulsory journey through every rock type.
Choose several paths, including a solid-state and a melting path.
The pathways connect processes at different depths and timescales; the animation does not assign one duration to the whole cycle.

glossary.def: Describing rock formed when magma or lava cools and crystallises. Slow cooling underground commonly produces larger crystals than rapid cooling at the surface. Texture therefore offers evidence of cooling history, although composition also affects the minerals present.

Describing rock formed from accumulated sediment or from chemical or biological precipitation. Clastic sediments commonly become rock through compaction and cementation. Bedding, grains and fossils can preserve evidence of the depositional environment.

Describing rock changed by heat, pressure or chemically active fluids while remaining mostly solid. New minerals or fabrics may develop. If the material melts and then crystallises, the resulting rock is igneous instead.

The conversion of loose sediment into solid sedimentary rock, commonly through compaction and cementation. Pressure reduces pore space, while minerals can precipitate between grains. Lithification does not normally require the sediment to melt.

A planar fabric in metamorphic rock, formed by aligned minerals or compositional bands. It commonly develops under directed stress. Foliation differs from sedimentary bedding, although both may appear as layers in an outcrop.
Partly or wholly molten rock beneath the surface, often containing crystals and dissolved gases. Molten rock erupted at the surface is called lava.

The breakdown or alteration of rock in place, supplying particles and dissolved material that may enter sedimentary pathways. Erosion then removes material, transport carries it, and deposition stores it elsewhere. These are connected processes rather than interchangeable names.

misconception.claim: Metamorphic rock forms when an existing rock melts completely.
misconception.truth: Metamorphism changes a rock’s minerals or texture while it remains largely solid, under changed temperature, pressure or fluid conditions. Complete melting produces magma; subsequent crystallisation forms igneous rock. The rock cycle includes different possible pathways rather than one compulsory sequence.

misconceptions.claim: Metamorphic rock forms when an existing rock melts completely.
misconceptions.truth: Metamorphism changes a rock’s minerals or texture while it remains largely solid, under changed temperature, pressure or fluid conditions. Complete melting produces magma; subsequent crystallisation forms igneous rock. The rock cycle includes different possible pathways rather than one compulsory sequence.

teacher.script:
Identify three rock groups, loose sediment and magma.

Choose several paths, including a solid-state and a melting path.
pitfalls: Distinguish molten material from igneous rock, which forms after the melt cools and solidifies.
Explain that some metamorphic rocks are foliated while others are not.
Consider composition and geological history alongside temperature and pressure when identifying a rock.

modelNotes: The pressure readout gives an equivalent depth using a uniform 2800 kg/m³ overburden and 9.81 m/s² gravity.

labs.title: Soil profile
labs.hook: A soil profile exposes horizons formed by organic inputs, weathering and material movement.
labs.objective: Identify the horizons in a soil profile and compare how water, organic matter and parent material influence their development.

steps.title: Observe
steps.body: Choose the temperate profile and read its depth scale. Name O, A, Bw and C; explain why E and R are not compulsory.

steps.title: Tinker
steps.body: Compare the dark mineral surface in the Mollisol example. Switch to Oxisol and discuss gradual boundaries and intense weathering.

steps.title: Explain
steps.body: How do the profiles show that a soil need not contain every possible horizon?

steps.title: Check
steps.body: Choose an answer and explain your reasoning. Each question includes feedback.

questions.explain: The R horizon is coherent bedrock beneath the soil and weathered parent material. Roots and water may enter its fractures, but it is not a loose soil horizon.

questions.prompt: A thick dark A is typical of…
questions.explain: Grassland roots supply organic matter through a substantial surface layer, and soil organisms mix it with mineral material. This helps form the thick, dark surface horizon characteristic of many Mollisols.
Oxisols develop under prolonged intense weathering and contain abundant iron and aluminium oxides. Many occur in tropical regions where warm, moist conditions promote deep chemical weathering.

choices: A leached, often paler eluviated layer
questions.explain: Eluviation removes materials such as clay, iron compounds or organic matter from the E horizon, often leaving it paler. An E horizon is not present in every soil profile.

why: A soil profile exposes horizons formed by organic inputs, weathering and material movement. Their colours and textures can provide clues, but not every soil contains every horizon.
Compare the dark mineral surface in the Mollisol example. Switch to Oxisol and discuss gradual boundaries and intense weathering.
The selected profiles are examples; identifying a soil order also requires diagnostic properties beyond a colour match.

glossary.def: A layer within a soil profile distinguished by properties such as colour, texture, organic matter or mineral accumulation. Horizons develop through soil-forming processes. Their boundaries can be gradual, and a real profile need not contain every named horizon.

A soil layer dominated by organic material such as leaf litter and decomposing plant remains. It may overlie mineral horizons in some soils but be absent in others. Its thickness depends on inputs, decomposition and disturbance.

The mineral soil layer near the surface, where organic matter mixes with sand, silt and clay. Its darker colour often reflects humus, but colour alone does not establish fertility or the depth of the layer.

A soil horizon depleted in materials such as clay, iron or organic compounds that have been carried away by percolating water. It often appears paler than adjacent layers. Not every soil profile contains a distinct E horizon.

A subsurface soil layer modified by soil-forming processes, often with an accumulation of clay or iron compounds moved from above. Compare its colour and structure with the A horizon; a B horizon is not simply any material beneath topsoil.

Hard bedrock beneath a soil profile. It differs from loose or partly weathered parent material usually labelled the C horizon. Roots and water may still penetrate joints even where the rock remains consolidated.
A USDA soil order characterised by a dark, base-rich surface horizon, often formed beneath grassland. It is not an exact synonym for every chernozem classification.

A deeply weathered soil order common in humid tropical regions, typically rich in iron and aluminium oxides. Long weathering and leaching can leave a low supply of readily available nutrients. A red colour alone is insufficient for classification.

misconception.claim: Every soil contains the same sequence and thickness of horizons.
misconception.truth: Soil profiles develop through interactions among parent material, climate, organisms, relief and time. Some horizons may be absent, weakly developed or altered by erosion and land use. Colour helps describe a profile, but classification also depends on diagnostic properties and processes.

misconceptions.claim: Every soil contains the same sequence and thickness of horizons.
misconceptions.truth: Soil profiles develop through interactions among parent material, climate, organisms, relief and time. Some horizons may be absent, weakly developed or altered by erosion and land use. Colour helps describe a profile, but classification also depends on diagnostic properties and processes.

teacher.script:
Choose the temperate profile and read its depth scale. Name O, A, Bw and C; explain why E and R are not compulsory.

Compare the dark mineral surface in the Mollisol example. Switch to Oxisol and discuss gradual boundaries and intense weathering.
pitfalls: Compare the selected profile with other environments rather than presenting it as a universal sequence of horizons.
Distinguish surface topsoil from the underlying horizons and from the bedrock represented by the R horizon.
Connect a deeply weathered tropical soil with its formation conditions rather than equating it with peat.

labs.title: Soil texture triangle
labs.hook: Soil texture describes the proportions of sand, silt and clay.
labs.objective: Use the proportions of sand, silt and clay to classify a soil, then explain how its texture affects water movement.

steps.title: Observe
steps.body: Read the sand, silt and clay axes and locate the selected mixture in the texture triangle. Check that its fractions add to 100%.

steps.title: Tinker
steps.body: Change the mixture and follow its position between texture classes. Explain how the particle sizes differ, then distinguish texture from soil structure.

steps.title: Explain
steps.body: Explain why changing one particle-size fraction requires at least one of the other fractions to change.

steps.title: Check
steps.body: Choose an answer and explain your reasoning. Each question includes feedback.

questions.explain: Clay is the smallest mineral particle-size fraction used in the soil texture triangle. Its large surface area and mineral properties help explain why many clay-rich soils are sticky when wet.

choices: A balanced mix near the middle — good for many farms
questions.explain: Loam occupies a texture class containing appreciable sand, silt and clay rather than being dominated by one extreme. Its mix can balance drainage and water retention, although soil productivity also depends on structure, nutrients and management.
With 90% sand, only 10% remains for silt and clay, placing the composition near the sand corner of the triangle. The precise sandy class depends on how that remaining fraction is divided.

questions.prompt: Sand, silt and clay on the triangle must…
questions.explain: Sand, silt and clay represent the complete mineral fine-earth sample classified by the triangle. Their percentages must total 100%, so increasing one fraction requires reducing one or both of the others.

why: Soil texture describes the proportions of sand, silt and clay. These fractions sum to 100%, and their mixture influences properties such as water retention and drainage.
Change the mixture and follow its position between texture classes. Explain how the particle sizes differ, then distinguish texture from soil structure.
Texture is one influence on soil behaviour; structure, organic matter and compaction also affect water movement.

glossary.def: In soil science, the proportions of sand, silt and clay in the mineral fraction. Texture influences pore sizes, drainage and water retention. It differs from soil structure, which describes how particles are arranged into aggregates.
Soil mineral particles 0.05–2 mm across in the USDA system. Other sediment classifications use a slightly different lower boundary.
Soil mineral particles 0.002–0.05 mm across in the USDA system, intermediate between clay and sand.
The finest soil mineral particles, less than 0.002 mm across in the USDA system. Their large surface area strongly affects water and nutrient retention.
A USDA soil-texture class containing a mixture of sand, silt and clay; loam is not defined as equal thirds of the three fractions.

A chart used to classify soil from its percentages of sand, silt and clay. The three fractions must add to 100%, and their intersection identifies a texture class. Texture describes particle size, while structure describes how particles form aggregates.

A triangular diagram showing three proportions whose sum is 100%. Each corner represents one pure component. In the soil-texture triangle, a sample’s sand, silt and clay percentages locate its texture class.

misconception.claim: A soil’s colour determines whether it is sand, silt or clay.
misconception.truth: Texture depends on the proportions of mineral particles in defined size classes. Colour reflects other properties, including organic matter, iron compounds and drainage conditions. Two soils can therefore look similar while having different textures, and texture differs from the way particles are grouped into structure.

misconceptions.claim: A soil’s colour determines whether it is sand, silt or clay.
misconceptions.truth: Texture depends on the proportions of mineral particles in defined size classes. Colour reflects other properties, including organic matter, iron compounds and drainage conditions. Two soils can therefore look similar while having different textures, and texture differs from the way particles are grouped into structure.

teacher.script:
Read the sand, silt and clay axes and locate the selected mixture in the texture triangle. Check that its fractions add to 100%.

Change the mixture and follow its position between texture classes. Explain how the particle sizes differ, then distinguish texture from soil structure.
pitfalls: Classify mineral texture using the proportions of sand, silt and clay, not the soil’s colour or a commercial label.
Check that the three mineral fractions total 100% before plotting a point on the triangle.
Explain that peat is dominated by organic material and is not a fourth corner of the mineral texture triangle.

modelNotes: The USDA texture triangle is a ternary plot: the three percentages must sum to 100.
Silt is the remainder so the three sum to 100.

labs.title: Weathering
labs.hook: Weathering changes rock in place.
labs.objective: Compare how freezing water, weakly acidic water and growing roots break down rock in place.

steps.title: Observe
steps.body: Choose Freezing and compare occupied volume before and after freezing. Compare physical scale and distinguish real opening from visual exaggeration.

steps.title: Tinker
steps.body: Choose Carbonate dissolution and read the reaction and mass balance. Compare Root growth, naming both mechanical and chemical biological effects.

steps.title: Explain
steps.body: How does each weathering process change rock in place, and what would be needed to transport the fragments away?

steps.title: Check
steps.body: Choose an answer and explain your reasoning. Each question includes feedback.

questions.explain: Water freezing within cracks, including the growth of ice as more water is drawn in, can exert stress on the surrounding rock. This breaks the rock physically without requiring a chemical change in its minerals.

choices: Carbonate rocks with weak carbonic acid
questions.explain: Carbon dioxide dissolved in water forms weak carbonic acid, which reacts with carbonate minerals. This dissolution helps enlarge fractures and form karst features in limestone.
Organisms can disrupt rock physically, for example through root growth, or chemically through acids and other compounds. Biological weathering therefore includes more than one breakdown mechanism.

choices: Weathering breaks in place; erosion moves the bits
questions.explain: Weathering alters or breaks down material where it is exposed. Erosion removes material from its original position through agents such as water, wind, ice or gravity.

why: Weathering changes rock in place. Freezing water, chemical dissolution and biological activity can weaken it through different mechanisms, often acting together before erosion transports the material.
Choose Carbonate dissolution and read the reaction and mass balance. Compare Root growth, naming both mechanical and chemical biological effects.
The demonstrations conserve the stated material quantities but prescribe the visible changes rather than calculating a universal weathering rate.

glossary.def: The physical breakdown of rock into smaller pieces without changing its mineral composition. Frost action and expansion or unloading can contribute. The fragments remain near their source until erosion transports them away.

The alteration or dissolution of minerals through chemical reactions with water, gases and dissolved substances. Carbonation, hydrolysis and oxidation are examples. Unlike mechanical weathering, these reactions change mineral composition as well as the appearance of the rock.

The breakdown or chemical alteration of rock caused by organisms. Roots can widen fractures, while organic acids from plants and microbes react with minerals. These effects overlap with mechanical and chemical weathering rather than forming an entirely separate mechanism.
Rock breakdown associated with freezing water and ice growth in cracks. Repeated freezing, thawing and ice segregation can widen the fractures.
Chemical weathering in which dissolved carbon dioxide forms weak carbonic acid that reacts with carbonate minerals such as calcite.
Physical breakdown or chemical alteration of rock at or near Earth's surface, without transporting the material away. Chemical weathering also participates in the carbon cycle.
The wearing away and removal of material by moving water, wind, ice or gravity. Weathering breaks down material in place.

misconception.claim: Chemical and mechanical weathering are separate alternatives that cannot act together.
misconception.truth: Several weathering processes can affect the same rock. Mechanical cracking exposes new surfaces to chemical reactions, while chemical alteration can weaken material for later breakage. Temperature, water, organisms and rock properties influence which processes are most effective in a particular setting.

misconceptions.claim: Chemical and mechanical weathering are separate alternatives that cannot act together.
misconceptions.truth: Several weathering processes can affect the same rock. Mechanical cracking exposes new surfaces to chemical reactions, while chemical alteration can weaken material for later breakage. Temperature, water, organisms and rock properties influence which processes are most effective in a particular setting.

teacher.script:
Choose Freezing and compare occupied volume before and after freezing. Compare physical scale and distinguish real opening from visual exaggeration.

Choose Carbonate dissolution and read the reaction and mass balance. Compare Root growth, naming both mechanical and chemical biological effects.
pitfalls: Distinguish weathering in place from erosion that removes and transports material.
Explain how water, temperature, organisms and rock type influence which weathering processes are effective.
Use a carbonate rock such as limestone to demonstrate carbonation rather than assuming all rocks react in the same way.

modelNotes: Using densities 1000 kg/m³ for liquid and 917 kg/m³ for ice, freezing increases occupied volume by about 9%.
The initial joint is 20 mm wide; the teaching view enlarges its change in opening tenfold, and Physical scale restores the real geometric change.
The readout conserves remaining solid plus dissolved calcite equivalent, using calcite density 2710 kg/m³.

labs.title: Soil erosion
labs.hook: Raindrops and flowing water can detach and carry soil.
labs.objective: Compare soil loss under different vegetation cover and explain how runoff carries sediment away from a slope.

steps.title: Observe
steps.body: Identify the bare and covered plots and the three sediment stores.

steps.title: Tinker
steps.body: Play or scrub; compare cover and then change the transport mechanism.

steps.title: Explain
steps.body: Why does detached sediment not necessarily leave the plot immediately?

steps.title: Check
steps.body: Choose an answer and explain your reasoning. Each question includes feedback.

choices: Always all material detached so far.
Material that has left the plot; some detached material may still be in transport.
The same thing as bedrock depth.
questions.explain: Detachment releases sediment from the soil, but that sediment may remain in motion or settle within the plot. Export counts only the material that crosses the plot boundary.

questions.prompt: The 85% reduction in this covered example is…
choices: An invented coefficient for a controlled comparison.
questions.explain: The 85% reduction is a chosen model coefficient that isolates the effect of cover in this comparison. A measured reduction would depend on soil, vegetation, rainfall, slope and management.

choices: The vertical display exaggeration of mean surface lowering.
questions.explain: The scale control changes how strongly the vertical surface lowering is exaggerated on screen. It leaves the calculated sediment transfers and their total unchanged.

why: Raindrops and flowing water can detach and carry soil. Ground cover reduces exposure and can slow transport, while deposited sediment remains within the catchment until it moves again.
Play or scrub; compare cover and then change the transport mechanism.
The selected sediment budget is a classroom comparison; local erosion rates require evidence about rainfall, soil and land management.

glossary.def: The detachment and movement of soil particles by raindrop impact. It can begin erosion before continuous runoff develops. Vegetation, litter and surface roughness reduce the direct impact on exposed mineral soil.

A small channel cut into soil by concentrated surface runoff. Rills can often be removed by ordinary cultivation, unlike larger gullies. They show that water has begun collecting into preferred routes rather than flowing as a broad sheet.

A channel cut into soil or unconsolidated material by concentrated runoff, larger and more persistent than a rill. In agricultural settings, a gully is generally too large to be removed by ordinary tillage and can expand through further erosion.

The removal of loose surface particles by wind. Fine material may be carried away in suspension, leaving a coarser lag behind. Deflation removes sediment; abrasion is the wearing of surfaces by particles that the wind carries.

The mineral soil layer near the surface, where organic matter mixes with sand, silt and clay. Its darker colour often reflects humus, but colour alone does not establish fertility or the depth of the layer.

Vegetation or plant residue that protects soil from direct raindrop impact and slows surface flow. Roots can also help hold particles together. The protective effect depends on the type, density and continuity of the cover.
Transport in short hops or bounces, especially of sand grains moved by wind or flowing water.

misconception.claim: Vegetation prevents all soil erosion.
misconception.truth: Plant cover can intercept raindrops, protect the soil and slow surface flow, reducing erosion. Its effectiveness depends on cover density, roots, soil condition, slope and the event itself. Even a vegetated slope can lose sediment during intense runoff or other disturbances.

misconceptions.claim: Vegetation prevents all soil erosion.
misconceptions.truth: Plant cover can intercept raindrops, protect the soil and slow surface flow, reducing erosion. Its effectiveness depends on cover density, roots, soil condition, slope and the event itself. Even a vegetated slope can lose sediment during intense runoff or other disturbances.

teacher.script:
Identify the bare and covered plots and the three sediment stores.

Play or scrub; compare cover and then change the transport mechanism.
pitfalls: Treat the selected coefficients as model inputs rather than measurements from a particular field.
Distinguish soil detached at the surface from sediment that is eventually exported from the plot.
Use the numerical readings for quantities; enlarged raindrops and grains help show the process rather than their actual sizes.

sources.label: NRCS RUSLE2: a different erosion-estimation method

modelNotes: Their invented active layer is 20 mm thick with dry bulk density 1500 kg/m³, giving 6000 kg per plot.
Every transfer is subtracted from one and added to another, so their sum stays at 6000 kg.
Play or scrub Process through 60 model minutes.
The chosen detachment coefficient is 0.004 per minute for rain and runoff, or 0.002 for dry wind; cover multiplies it by 0.15.
Sediment leaves the transport store at 0.15 or 0.3 per minute respectively.
Its usual display is enlarged 30 times; Physical scale restores actual lowering.

labs.title: Earthquakes
labs.hook: An earthquake releases energy when rock slips along a fault.
labs.objective: Locate the focus and epicentre of an earthquake and compare how different seismic waves travel through Earth.

steps.title: Observe
steps.body: Identify hypocentre, epicentre and the separate fault trace. Set Focus depth to 20 km and predict which front reaches the station first.

steps.title: Tinker
steps.body: Scrub Process through both arrivals and read the times. Increase depth, then explain the longer ray path.

steps.title: Explain
steps.body: How does increasing the focus depth change the wave path and arrival time at a fixed station?

steps.title: Check
steps.body: Choose an answer and explain your reasoning. Each question includes feedback.

choices: The point of slip in the rock
questions.explain: The focus is the location inside Earth where earthquake rupture begins. The epicentre is the point on the surface directly above it.

choices: Are fastest and travel through solid and liquid
questions.explain: P-waves transmit alternating compression and expansion, which both solids and liquids can support. They are the fastest major seismic wave type and usually arrive first.

choices: Often do the damage at the surface, arriving later
questions.explain: Love and Rayleigh waves travel along Earth's surface and can produce large, sustained ground motion. They arrive after the faster body waves and can contribute substantially to damage.

choices: Magnitude is the source size; intensity is what a place feels
Intensity is only at the focus
questions.explain: Magnitude measures the size of the earthquake source, while intensity describes shaking and effects at a particular location. One earthquake can therefore produce different intensities at different sites.

why: An earthquake releases energy when rock slips along a fault. The focus is the source at depth and the epicentre lies above it; different seismic waves transmit the disturbance through and along Earth.
Scrub Process through both arrivals and read the times. Increase depth, then explain the longer ray path.
The wave illustration separates propagation mechanisms; shaking and damage also depend on the source, distance, ground and buildings.

glossary.def: The point within Earth where an earthquake rupture starts, also called the hypocentre. Rupture can then spread across a much larger fault surface. The epicentre is the point directly above it at the surface.

The point on Earth’s surface directly above the focus of an earthquake. It helps locate an event on a map, but the strongest shaking may occur elsewhere because of fault rupture, distance and local ground conditions.
A compressional seismic wave with particle motion parallel to its travel direction. It travels through solids and liquids and is the faster body-wave type.
A shear seismic wave with particle motion perpendicular to its travel direction. It propagates through solids but not through the liquid outer core.

A seismic wave that travels along Earth’s surface, including Love and Rayleigh waves. These waves can produce strong, prolonged ground motion, although damage also depends on frequency, distance, ground conditions and buildings. They differ from body waves travelling through Earth.

A measure of an earthquake’s overall size, commonly reported as moment magnitude based on fault area, slip and rock rigidity. One event has a magnitude, while its shaking intensity varies from place to place. The scale is logarithmic.
The strength of earthquake shaking and its effects at a particular place. It depends on the earthquake, distance, local ground and built structures.

misconception.claim: Earthquake magnitude and shaking intensity are the same measurement.
misconception.truth: Magnitude describes the earthquake’s size at its source. Intensity describes shaking and effects at a particular place, so it varies with distance, local ground and buildings. One earthquake can therefore have a single reported magnitude but many different local intensities.

misconceptions.claim: Earthquake magnitude and shaking intensity are the same measurement.
misconceptions.truth: Magnitude describes the earthquake’s size at its source. Intensity describes shaking and effects at a particular place, so it varies with distance, local ground and buildings. One earthquake can therefore have a single reported magnitude but many different local intensities.

teacher.script:
Identify hypocentre, epicentre and the separate fault trace. Set Focus depth to 20 km and predict which front reaches the station first.

Scrub Process through both arrivals and read the times. Increase depth, then explain the longer ray path.
pitfalls: Distinguish earthquake magnitude from the intensity of shaking experienced at a particular location.
Locate the epicentre at the surface above the focus, and explain that S waves do not pass through the liquid outer core.
Identify the fault setting before interpreting an event; California includes transform movement as well as other tectonic settings.

modelNotes: P fronts expand at 6 km/s and S fronts at 3.5 km/s.
Play or scrub Process through 25 seconds and change Focus depth.
Compare P and S arrivals at the station 50 km horizontally from the epicentre; the straight-ray distance is √(depth² + 50²).
The violet surface front is a simplified illustration launched when S first reaches the epicentre and travelling at 3.2 km/s.

labs.title: Volcanoes
labs.hook: Magma composition, gas content and the conditions of ascent influence eruption style.
labs.objective: Explain how magma viscosity influences volcanic form and eruption style, using shield and composite volcanoes as examples.

steps.title: Observe
steps.body: Compare the broad shield and steeper composite cone. Name viscosity as one influence on lava flow. Raise Gas drive independently. Basalt can fragment too; gas and external water matter.

steps.title: Tinker
steps.body: Switch to Fissure vents. A fissure is a crack, not a viscosity class. Open the cross-section and identify the conduit.

steps.title: Explain
steps.body: Explain why viscosity alone cannot determine whether an eruption fragments magma or produces flowing lava.

steps.title: Check
steps.body: Choose an answer and explain your reasoning. Each question includes feedback.

choices: Low-viscosity basalt, long flows, gentle slopes
questions.explain: Low-viscosity basaltic lava can travel far from a vent before solidifying. Repeated spreading flows build the broad, gently sloping form of a shield volcano.

choices: Stickier, gassier magma builds layers of lava and ash
questions.explain: More viscous lava tends to travel shorter distances, while explosive eruptions add layers of fragmented material. Repeated eruptions can therefore build a relatively steep composite cone.

choices: Can be a fissure of basalt at a divergent boundary
questions.explain: Extension at a divergent boundary opens fractures and allows magma to rise. Basalt may then erupt along an elongated fissure rather than from a single central vent.

questions.prompt: Sticky magma explodes more readily because…
choices: Gas cannot escape easily, so pressure builds
questions.explain: Viscous magma can impede gas escape as pressure falls during ascent. Expanding trapped gas can then fragment the magma and drive an explosive eruption, although viscosity is only one control.

why: Magma composition, gas content and the conditions of ascent influence eruption style. Comparing volcanic forms helps connect those processes with lava flows, fragmental deposits and the structure built over time.
Switch to Fissure vents. A fissure is a crack, not a viscosity class. Open the cross-section and identify the conduit.
The displayed eruptions illustrate selected mechanisms; volcano shape alone cannot predict the next eruption.

glossary.def: A measure of a fluid’s resistance to deformation and flow. Magma viscosity depends on composition, temperature and crystal content. More viscous magma can hinder gas escape, but eruption style also depends on gas supply, ascent and interaction with external water.
A broad volcano with gentle slopes built mainly by fluid lava flows, commonly basaltic. Mauna Loa is a classic example.
A commonly steep-sided volcano built from successive lava flows and fragmental deposits. Its magma composition and eruption style can vary; many form above subduction zones.

An eruption in which magma emerges along an elongated crack rather than only from a single central vent. Lava fountains may form a line and then become concentrated at a few outlets. Basaltic fissure eruptions are common in Iceland and Hawaiʻi.
A fine-grained volcanic rock rich in iron- and magnesium-bearing minerals. Basaltic magma is generally less viscous than silica-rich magma.
A passage through which magma and volcanic gases rise towards an eruptive vent.

Describing fragmented volcanic material ejected during an explosive eruption, including ash, lapilli and larger blocks. Pyroclastic deposits differ from coherent lava flows. Particle size and deposit structure help reconstruct how material was transported.

misconception.claim: A volcano’s size alone predicts how explosive its next eruption will be.
misconception.truth: Eruption behaviour depends on magma properties, gas, ascent conditions and possible interaction with water or ice. Large shield volcanoes often produce fluid lava flows, but basaltic eruptions can also be explosive. The existing landform records earlier activity without determining every future event.

misconceptions.claim: A volcano’s size alone predicts how explosive its next eruption will be.
misconceptions.truth: Eruption behaviour depends on magma properties, gas, ascent conditions and possible interaction with water or ice. Large shield volcanoes often produce fluid lava flows, but basaltic eruptions can also be explosive. The existing landform records earlier activity without determining every future event.

teacher.script:
Compare the broad shield and steeper composite cone. Name viscosity as one influence on lava flow. Raise Gas drive independently. Basalt can fragment too; gas and external water matter.

Switch to Fissure vents. A fissure is a crack, not a viscosity class. Open the cross-section and identify the conduit.
pitfalls: Compare effusive and explosive activity rather than assuming every volcano erupts in the same way.
Include hotspot and divergent-boundary examples as well as volcanoes around subduction zones.
Explain how repeated fluid lava flows build a shield volcano rather than describing it as an eroded stratovolcano.

labs.title: Tsunami
labs.hook: A tsunami has a long wavelength and travels faster in deeper water.
labs.objective: Explain how seafloor displacement generates a tsunami and why its speed and height change as it enters shallow water.

steps.title: Observe
steps.body: Scrub the first source stage and explain water displacement, contrasting it with wind-driven surge. Continue to the separate propagation approximation and follow the prescribed wave packet.

steps.title: Tinker
steps.body: Read the same front’s speed in deep and shallow water. Use the metre-scale chart to compare amplitudes.

steps.title: Explain
steps.body: How does decreasing water depth change the speed and height of a long wave approaching the coast?

steps.title: Check
steps.body: Choose an answer and explain your reasoning. Each question includes feedback.

choices: A sudden shift of the water column, often seafloor slip
questions.explain: A tsunami begins when a large volume of water is displaced rapidly, often by vertical movement of the seafloor during an earthquake. Landslides and other disturbances can also generate tsunamis.

questions.prompt: In deep water a tsunami is…
choices: Fast and often unnoticed at sea
questions.explain: A tsunami's long wavelength allows it to travel rapidly through deep water while its offshore height may remain small. A ship can therefore experience little noticeable change even as the wave passes.

questions.prompt: It grows at the coast because…
choices: Shoaling: energy in a shallower, slower water column
questions.explain: As a tsunami enters shallower water, it slows and its wavelength shortens. Its height can increase through shoaling, with the final coastal response also shaped by refraction, seabed geometry and energy loss.

questions.prompt: Katrina and Sandy’s water at the coast was…
choices: Storm surge from wind and pressure, not seafloor slip
questions.explain: Katrina and Sandy raised coastal water levels through storm winds and atmospheric pressure, combined with tides and waves. That storm-surge mechanism differs from the rapid water-column displacement that generates a tsunami.

why: A tsunami has a long wavelength and travels faster in deeper water. As it crosses into shallower water, it slows and its amplitude can increase as energy is concentrated into a smaller depth.
Read the same front’s speed in deep and shallow water. Use the metre-scale chart to compare amplitudes.
This long-wave calculation ends offshore and excludes breaking, run-up and inundation on land.

glossary.def: A series of long waves generated by rapid displacement of water, most commonly during a large undersea earthquake. In shallow water they slow and can grow in height. Tsunamis are not caused by the normal daily tides.
The change in a wave as it enters shallower water: it slows, its wavelength shortens, and its height may increase before breaking.

A rise in sea level above the expected tide, driven mainly by storm winds and atmospheric pressure. Coastal shape and water depth influence its size. Surge combines with tides and waves to determine coastal water levels and flooding.
A large, low-angle thrust fault at a subduction boundary. Sudden slip on its shallow offshore part can displace the seafloor and generate a tsunami.

The distance between corresponding points on successive waves, such as one crest and the next. A tsunami has a very long wavelength compared with ordinary wind waves. Its wavelength changes as speed and water depth change during propagation.

A lowering of water level. In the tsunami lab it means the withdrawal of the sea before some waves; many tsunami arrive without this warning. Groundwater drawdown means a lowered water table or pressure level.
The maximum elevation reached by a wave above a specified reference sea level as it moves onto land; distinct from inland inundation distance.

misconception.claim: A tsunami and a storm surge are the same kind of coastal wave.
misconception.truth: A tsunami is a sequence of long waves generated by rapid water displacement, such as seafloor movement or a landslide. Storm surge is an abnormal water-level rise driven mainly by storm winds and atmospheric pressure. Their causes, propagation and warning evidence differ.

misconceptions.claim: A tsunami and a storm surge are the same kind of coastal wave.
misconceptions.truth: A tsunami is a sequence of long waves generated by rapid water displacement, such as seafloor movement or a landslide. Storm surge is an abnormal water-level rise driven mainly by storm winds and atmospheric pressure. Their causes, propagation and warning evidence differ.

teacher.script:
Scrub the first source stage and explain water displacement, contrasting it with wind-driven surge. Continue to the separate propagation approximation and follow the prescribed wave packet.

Read the same front’s speed in deep and shallow water. Use the metre-scale chart to compare amplitudes.
pitfalls: Distinguish a tsunami from astronomical tides and wind-driven storm surge, including the 1953 North Sea event.
Explain why a tsunami can have a small wave height in deep water and change greatly as it enters shallow water.
Connect coastal flooding to the generating process instead of identifying the hazard from water level alone.

modelNotes: The propagation experiment starts with a prescribed 20-minute wave packet and 0.5 m deep-water amplitude.
Along a 500 km transect, depth declines gradually from 4000 m to 100 m.
The first 15% of Process prescribes up to 1 m of seafloor uplift and displaces the overlying water column; the gold arrow magnifies the direction.
The 3D wave height uses the same vertical scale as bathymetry, enlarged twentyfold in the teaching view.
Gradually varying depth, no reflection and no lateral spreading are strong assumptions; the transect ends in 100 m water before the coast.

labs.title: Tropical cyclone
labs.hook: A tropical cyclone draws moist air inward near the surface, with strong ascent in the eyewall and outflow aloft.
labs.objective: Identify the eye, eyewall and rainbands of a tropical cyclone and explain how warm ocean water supports its circulation.

steps.title: Observe
steps.body: Locate eye, eyewall and rainbands. Trace inflow, ascent and outflow, distinguishing subsidence in the eye.

steps.title: Tinker
steps.body: Read the wind profile and its 30 km maximum. Change Intensity; explain why the pressure is model-dependent.

steps.title: Explain
steps.body: How are the strongest winds near the eyewall related to the pressure change towards the centre?

steps.title: Check
steps.body: Choose an answer and explain your reasoning. Each question includes feedback.

choices: The ring of strongest winds and rain around the eye
questions.explain: The eyewall surrounds the relatively calm eye and contains vigorous rising air and deep convection. The strongest near-surface winds commonly occur in or close to this ring.

choices: Warm ocean and low shear, among other things
questions.explain: Warm ocean water can supply heat and moisture, while low vertical wind shear helps organised convection remain aligned with the circulation. These favourable conditions do not by themselves guarantee that a cyclone will develop.

questions.prompt: A UK winter storm is usually…
questions.explain: UK winter storms are usually extratropical cyclones associated with contrasts between air masses and with fronts. Their structure and energy sources differ from those of a tropical cyclone over warm water.

choices: Tropical cyclones, not UK extra-tropical gales
questions.explain: The Saffir–Simpson scale assigns hurricane categories using maximum sustained wind speed. It does not classify ordinary UK extratropical gales or represent a storm's rainfall and surge hazards.

why: A tropical cyclone draws moist air inward near the surface, with strong ascent in the eyewall and outflow aloft. Its eye has weaker winds and often descending air, distinct from a tornado funnel.
Read the wind profile and its 30 km maximum. Change Intensity; explain why the pressure is model-dependent.
The ideal vortex links wind and pressure through stated assumptions; it does not calculate storm development, rainfall or a track.

glossary.def: An organised, rotating low-pressure system with a warm core that develops over tropical or subtropical water. Strong storms can form an eye and eyewall. Hurricanes and typhoons are regional names for the same class of storm.

The relatively calm central region of a developed tropical cyclone, often with sinking air and reduced cloud. The surrounding eyewall contains much more vigorous convection and stronger winds. Passing into the eye does not mean that the storm has ended.

The ring of deep convection around a tropical cyclone’s eye, usually containing its strongest winds and heaviest rainfall. Its position and structure can change as the storm evolves. It differs from the calmer eye and the outer spiral rainbands.

An elongated or curved band of showers and thunderstorms within a storm system. Tropical cyclones commonly have spiral rainbands outside the eyewall. Their rainfall and winds can affect locations well beyond the eye, with large variation between storms.

A rise in sea level above the expected tide, driven mainly by storm winds and atmospheric pressure. Coastal shape and water depth influence its size. Surge combines with tides and waves to determine coastal water levels and flooding.
A five-category hurricane scale based on maximum sustained wind speed. It does not rate rainfall, storm surge or the full impact of a cyclone.
An extratropical low-pressure system that develops from contrasts in temperature and is commonly associated with warm and cold fronts.

misconception.claim: The calm eye means a tropical cyclone has passed and the danger is over.
misconception.truth: The eye is surrounded by the eyewall, where winds and convection are strong. If the eye crosses a location, the opposite eyewall may arrive after a temporary lull, with a changed wind direction. Rainfall, flooding and coastal water levels can also remain hazardous beyond the strongest winds.

misconceptions.claim: The calm eye means a tropical cyclone has passed and the danger is over.
misconceptions.truth: The eye is surrounded by the eyewall, where winds and convection are strong. If the eye crosses a location, the opposite eyewall may arrive after a temporary lull, with a changed wind direction. Rainfall, flooding and coastal water levels can also remain hazardous beyond the strongest winds.

teacher.script:
Locate eye, eyewall and rainbands. Trace inflow, ascent and outflow, distinguishing subsidence in the eye.

Read the wind profile and its 30 km maximum. Change Intensity; explain why the pressure is model-dependent.
pitfalls: Distinguish a tropical cyclone from a midlatitude windstorm and apply intensity scales only to the storms they describe.
Locate the strongest winds around the eyewall rather than in the relatively calm eye.
Explain storm surge as a rise in sea level driven by the storm, separate from both tsunami waves and ordinary wind waves.

modelNotes: The ideal wind profile increases linearly from a calm centre to a maximum at radius 30 km, then decreases inversely with radius.
Intensity selects maximum tangential wind from 38 to 80 m/s.
A steady radial gradient-wind balance uses constant density 1.15 kg/m³, Coriolis magnitude 0.00005 per second and outer pressure 101300 Pa at 300 km.
Cloud depth is 12 km, enlarged fivefold until T is pressed; cloud particles are visual volumes, not simulated droplets or rainfall.

labs.title: Graticule and coordinates
labs.hook: Latitude measures an angle north or south of the equator, while longitude measures an angle east or west of the prime meridian.
labs.objective: Use latitude and longitude to locate a point on Earth, and relate longitude to differences in local solar time.

steps.title: Observe
steps.body: Locate the equator and prime meridian, then follow a parallel and a meridian around the globe.

steps.title: Tinker
steps.body: Change Latitude first, then Longitude. Read the hemisphere letters and explain why changing one coordinate moves the marker along a different direction.

steps.title: Explain
steps.body: Why does one degree of longitude cover less ground near the poles than near the equator?

steps.title: Check
steps.body: Choose an answer and explain your reasoning. Each question includes feedback.

choices: Angle from the equator, 0° to 90° N or S
questions.explain: Latitude locates a point north or south of the equator using an angle up to 90°. Lines of equal latitude are parallels, with the North Pole at 90° N.
The prime meridian is the agreed zero reference from which longitude is measured east or west. Choosing that reference is a mapping convention rather than a physical boundary on Earth.
Earth turns through 360° relative to the Sun during a mean solar day of 24 hours. Dividing gives about 15° of longitude for each hour of local solar-time difference.

choices: In the Atlantic, south of Ghana, where equator meets Greenwich
questions.explain: Zero latitude identifies the equator and zero longitude identifies the prime meridian. Their intersection lies in the Gulf of Guinea in the Atlantic Ocean, south of Ghana.

why: Latitude measures an angle north or south of the equator, while longitude measures an angle east or west of the prime meridian. Parallels and meridians form the coordinate grid called the graticule.
Change Latitude first, then Longitude. Read the hemisphere letters and explain why changing one coordinate moves the marker along a different direction.
These are angular coordinates on a sphere; a degree of longitude covers less ground as latitude increases.

glossary.def: The network of meridians and parallels on a globe or map.

A line of longitude running from one pole to the other. A place’s local solar noon occurs when the Sun crosses its local meridian. Meridians meet at the poles, so the distance between adjacent longitudes decreases towards high latitudes.

A line joining places at the same latitude. On a spherical globe, the equator is the largest parallel and the others become smaller towards the poles. Parallels do not intersect, unlike meridians of longitude, which meet at the poles.

The angular position of a place north or south of the equator, expressed in degrees. Latitude helps determine solar altitude and seasonal day length. Lines of equal latitude are parallels, unlike meridians, which measure longitude.

The angular position of a place east or west of the prime meridian, expressed up to 180 degrees. Earth turns through approximately 15 degrees per hour, linking longitude with local solar time. Civil time zones also reflect administrative choices.
The chosen zero of longitude. The modern reference meridian used by WGS84 lies about 102 m east of the historic Greenwich transit circle.

The circle at zero degrees latitude, halfway between the poles. It divides Earth into Northern and Southern Hemispheres. It is a parallel of latitude, whereas meridians of longitude run from pole to pole.

The conventional boundary across which the civil calendar date changes, located broadly near 180 degrees longitude. Its course bends around countries and islands for practical reasons. It differs from the prime meridian, which defines zero longitude.

misconception.claim: The coordinates 0 degrees latitude and 0 degrees longitude locate Greenwich.
misconception.truth: Greenwich is close to zero longitude but about 51.5 degrees north of the equator. Zero latitude lies on the equator, so the two zero coordinates meet in the Gulf of Guinea. Latitude and longitude identify separate angular directions and must both be specified.

misconceptions.claim: The coordinates 0 degrees latitude and 0 degrees longitude locate Greenwich.
misconceptions.truth: Greenwich is close to zero longitude but about 51.5 degrees north of the equator. Zero latitude lies on the equator, so the two zero coordinates meet in the Gulf of Guinea. Latitude and longitude identify separate angular directions and must both be specified.

teacher.script:
Locate the equator and prime meridian, then follow a parallel and a meridian around the globe.

Change Latitude first, then Longitude. Read the hemisphere letters and explain why changing one coordinate moves the marker along a different direction.
pitfalls: Check the east–west convention using a known location; New York is west of Greenwich.
Distinguish the prime meridian from the International Date Line, and place 0° latitude, 0° longitude on the equator.
Explain that time zones are human conventions for clocks, while Earth’s rotation produces day and night.

modelNotes: US Eastern, Central, Mountain, and Pacific are four civil labels across about 60° of longitude; the terminator ignores the jogs around state lines.
A Leeds frost at 07:00 is already sunlight on a Berlin school roof.
Railways forced time zones onto 15° meridians.
The equator does none of that work: it is 0° latitude, a different axis of the same net.
Latitude is the angle from the equator, 0° to 90° north or south.
Longitude is the angle from the Greenwich meridian, 0° to 180° east or west.
The equator is 0° latitude, not a line of longitude.
Greenwich is 0° longitude, a convention; the spin does not care which meridian we labelled zero.

labs.title: Map projections
labs.hook: A map projection transfers positions from a curved surface to a plane.
labs.objective: Compare how map projections represent a curved Earth on a flat surface, identifying the distortions each introduces.

steps.title: Observe
steps.body: Compare Greenland and Africa on the globe before flattening it. Predict which properties may change on the map.

steps.title: Tinker
steps.body: Flatten each projection fully. Compare the equal-sized circles at low and high latitudes, then describe the trade-off between area and shape.

steps.title: Explain
steps.body: Choose a map use and explain which distortion would matter most for that purpose.

steps.title: Check
steps.body: Choose an answer and explain your reasoning. Each question includes feedback.

questions.prompt: On a Mercator world map Greenland looks…
choices: About the size of Africa — a distortion; Africa is far larger
The same as on the globe
questions.explain: Mercator's scale increases strongly towards the poles, enlarging high-latitude areas on the map. Greenland therefore appears far larger relative to Africa than its actual area warrants.

questions.prompt: An equal-area projection is built to…
questions.explain: An equal-area projection preserves area ratios between mapped regions. Flattening the curved surface still requires distortion of other properties, including local shapes or distances.

questions.prompt: Why do we still use Mercator at sea historically?
questions.explain: A rhumb line maintains a constant compass bearing, and Mercator represents it as a straight line. This property made the projection useful for plotting sailing directions even though it distorts area.

questions.prompt: The globe in this lab is the…
choices: Reference: a sphere (almost) does not need a projection
questions.explain: A globe represents positions on a curved surface without first flattening them onto a plane. Comparing it with a flat map reveals the distortions introduced by the projection.

why: A map projection transfers positions from a curved surface to a plane. Every projection distorts some combination of area, shape, distance and direction, so the right choice depends on the map’s purpose.
Flatten each projection fully. Compare the equal-sized circles at low and high latitudes, then describe the trade-off between area and shape.
Judge each projection when it is fully flat; intermediate shapes are a visual transition rather than a separate projection.

glossary.def: A mathematical method for representing positions on a curved surface on a flat map. Every world projection changes some combination of area, shape, distance or direction. Its suitability depends on which properties matter for the map’s intended use.

A conformal cylindrical map projection on which constant compass bearings plot as straight lines. It is useful for some navigation tasks, but areas become greatly enlarged towards the poles. Apparent land areas on it should not be compared directly.

Describing a projection that preserves the relative areas of regions on a map. Shapes and angles must be distorted to achieve this on a flat surface. Equal-area maps are useful when comparing the size or distribution of geographic regions.

Describing a map projection that preserves local angles and small shapes. This is useful for bearings, but area can become strongly distorted over a world map. A conformal projection cannot also preserve the area of every region.
A path of constant compass bearing, shown as a straight line on a Mercator map. Except for special cases, it is not the shortest path on a sphere.
Tapered strips of a map designed to be fitted around a globe; small strips reduce the distortion needed to cover a sphere.
A map projection that balances several kinds of distortion without preserving any one property exactly everywhere.
A change in area, shape, distance or direction caused by projecting a curved surface onto a plane. No flat world map preserves all of them everywhere.

misconception.claim: One flat world map can preserve every area, shape, distance and direction.
misconception.truth: Flattening Earth’s curved surface necessarily introduces distortion. A projection may preserve a selected property, such as area, while changing others. Compare a map with a globe and choose its projection according to the task, rather than assuming all visual comparisons are equally reliable.

misconceptions.claim: One flat world map can preserve every area, shape, distance and direction.
misconceptions.truth: Flattening Earth’s curved surface necessarily introduces distortion. A projection may preserve a selected property, such as area, while changing others. Compare a map with a globe and choose its projection according to the task, rather than assuming all visual comparisons are equally reliable.

cases.label: Greenwich as a meridian, not a map

teacher.script:
Compare Greenland and Africa on the globe before flattening it. Predict which properties may change on the map.

Flatten each projection fully. Compare the equal-sized circles at low and high latitudes, then describe the trade-off between area and shape.
pitfalls: Compare the properties a projection preserves with those it distorts before choosing it for a task.
Use the globe to check area comparisons, including the enlarged appearance of Greenland on a Mercator map.
Distinguish the requirements of a world map from those of a local map covering a much smaller region.

modelNotes: The surface uses mapped Earth imagery and mathematical projection formulas, limited to 85 degrees north and south to avoid the Mercator pole singularities.

labs.title: Grid references
labs.hook: A grid reference locates a cell using eastings followed by northings.
labs.objective: Read and plot a six-figure grid reference by locating the easting before the northing.

steps.title: Observe
steps.body: Read the board’s scale and locate its eastings and northings. Distinguish the full 100 km square from a selected 100 m cell.

steps.title: Tinker
steps.body: Set Easting before Northing and read the six-figure reference. Add the letter pair when explaining how a full British National Grid reference identifies the wider square.

steps.title: Explain
steps.body: Explain the difference between identifying a grid square and measuring a point’s position accurately.

steps.title: Check
steps.body: Choose an answer and explain your reasoning. Each question includes feedback.

choices: Eastings then northings — along the corridor, up the stairs
questions.explain: Eastings identify the position across the grid and northings identify the position up it. Giving them in that order ensures that both coordinates refer to the intended square or location.

questions.prompt: A six-figure reference locates to about…
questions.explain: A six-figure grid reference uses three digits for each direction, identifying a 100 m square within the kilometre grid. It indicates a smaller area than a four-figure reference rather than an exact point.

choices: The 1 km square whose SW corner is easting 12, northing 34
questions.explain: The first pair of digits identifies the western grid line and the second identifies the southern grid line. Together they locate the 1 km square extending northeast from that southwest corner.

choices: A projected kilometre grid on Great Britain
questions.explain: The British National Grid projects positions onto a flat coordinate system expressed in metres. It supports grid distances and references, while latitude and longitude describe angular position on Earth.

why: A grid reference locates a cell using eastings followed by northings. More digits identify a smaller cell, while the letter pair identifies its wider British National Grid square.
Set Easting before Northing and read the six-figure reference. Add the letter pair when explaining how a full British National Grid reference identifies the wider square.
The board is fictional, and a more precise reference does not by itself make a measurement more accurate.

glossary.def: A grid coordinate measuring distance east from a defined origin. Read eastings before northings in a grid reference.

A map-grid coordinate measuring distance north from the grid’s defined origin. Read it after the easting when giving a grid reference. The coordinate locates a position within a projected grid; it is not the same quantity as latitude.

A reference identifying a 1 km square on a standard British National Grid map by its southwest corner. Read the easting first and then the northing. It identifies a square, not an exact point within it.

A reference locating a 100 m square within a standard British National Grid kilometre square. Read three easting figures before three northing figures. Adding figures improves reference precision, but the map and observation still limit accuracy.
Ordnance Survey Great Britain. OSGB36 is a geodetic datum used with the British National Grid; it differs from the global WGS84 reference system.
An offset origin used to keep map-grid coordinates convenient and usually positive. The British National Grid uses one southwest of Great Britain.
An area identified by a map grid. In British National Grid notation, four, six and eight figures identify 1 km, 100 m and 10 m squares respectively.
A global geodetic reference system used by GPS, including a reference ellipsoid and coordinate frame. Converting to the British National Grid requires a projection and datum transformation.

misconception.claim: A six-figure British National Grid reference identifies an exact point.
misconception.truth: A six-figure reference identifies a 100-metre square within the relevant lettered grid square. More digits specify a smaller area, but extra precision does not guarantee an accurate observation. Read eastings before northings and include the letter pair when the wider location is needed.

misconceptions.claim: A six-figure British National Grid reference identifies an exact point.
misconceptions.truth: A six-figure reference identifies a 100-metre square within the relevant lettered grid square. More digits specify a smaller area, but extra precision does not guarantee an accurate observation. Read eastings before northings and include the letter pair when the wider location is needed.

teacher.script:
Read the board’s scale and locate its eastings and northings. Distinguish the full 100 km square from a selected 100 m cell.

Set Easting before Northing and read the six-figure reference. Add the letter pair when explaining how a full British National Grid reference identifies the wider square.
pitfalls: Read eastings before northings and distinguish the projected grid from latitude and longitude.
Explain that a six-figure reference identifies a 100 m square rather than an exact point within it.
Check the coordinate system before comparing an OS grid reference with a GPS location.

modelNotes: A complete short reference needs the 100 km letter pair followed by eastings and northings.
Six figures identify a 100 m square, not a surveyed point accurate to one metre.
Four figures such as 1234 identify the 1 km square with southwest corner at easting 12 and northing 34.
Six figures subdivide to 100 m, and eight figures to 10 m.
This fictional board spans one 100 by 100 km square; its main grid lines are 10 km apart.

labs.title: Mass movement
labs.hook: Gravity drives a slope downhill while friction and cohesion resist movement.
labs.objective: Identify the main parts of a rotational slump and explain how rainfall can reduce the stability of a slope.

steps.title: Observe
steps.body: Locate crown, curved shear surface and toe. Read the assumed strength and initial factor of safety.

steps.title: Tinker
steps.body: Increase Pore pressure and relate falling resistance to effective stress. At the highest setting, play the prescribed rotational movement.

steps.title: Explain
steps.body: How does increasing pore pressure reduce the resistance to sliding along the selected surface?

steps.title: Check
steps.body: Choose an answer and explain your reasoning. Each question includes feedback.

choices: A curved shear surface, like a spoon scoop
questions.explain: A rotational slump moves along a curved slip surface, so the displaced block rotates as it descends. The head drops and may tilt backwards while material moves outward near the toe.

questions.prompt: Rain makes till more likely to fail because…
choices: Pore water pressure reduces effective strength
questions.explain: Higher pore-water pressure reduces the effective stress pressing soil particles together. This weakens frictional resistance and can make a slope more likely to fail.

questions.prompt: After pore pressure rises enough that the selected factor of safety is below one, Play shows…
choices: A prescribed rotation: the head drops and the toe moves outward.
questions.explain: A factor of safety below one means the selected driving forces exceed the model's resisting forces. The displayed rotation illustrates that unstable condition but does not predict the real rate or displacement of a slide.

questions.prompt: Before comparing a real coastal slide with this model, check…
choices: Whether its material, pore pressure and slip geometry support a rotational mechanism.
questions.explain: Material strength, pore pressure and the geometry of the failure surface determine whether a rotational mechanism is plausible. Two coastal slopes can fail differently despite sharing a similar setting.

why: Gravity drives a slope downhill while friction and cohesion resist movement. Rising pore-water pressure can reduce effective stress and resistance, making a chosen slip surface less stable.
Increase Pore pressure and relate falling resistance to effective stress. At the highest setting, play the prescribed rotational movement.
The factor of safety describes the initial slope and selected surface; the later rotation is an illustration of movement, not a calculated runout.

glossary.def: A landslide in which a mass of soil or rock rotates along a curved slip surface. The upper part commonly drops and tilts back, while material moves outward near the toe. Water pressure can reduce the slope’s resistance to failure.

A surface along which adjacent masses move relative to each other. In a landslide it separates moving material from the underlying slope and may be curved or nearly planar. It is distinct from the exposed cliff or landslide scar.

The upper edge of a landslide, where displaced material separates from stable ground. Cracks near the crown can outline the developing failure. It is distinct from the toe, where displaced material accumulates farther down the slope.
The downslope end of a landslide or other mass-movement deposit. Displaced material may thicken or bulge there as it slows. It differs from the crown, where material separates from the stable slope.
The pressure of water or gas within pores in soil or rock. Increasing water pressure can reduce effective stress and resistance to slope failure.

Unsorted sediment deposited directly by glacier ice, often containing a mixture from clay to boulders. Its poor sorting distinguishes it from many meltwater deposits reworked by flowing water. Till can form several types of glacial landform.

The downslope movement of rock or soil under gravity, including falls, slides and flows. Water can increase weight or pore pressure and may be mixed with the moving material. Gravity provides the driving force rather than a transporting river or wind.

misconception.claim: Rain can destabilise a slope only by making the material heavier.
misconception.truth: Added water can increase weight, but rising pore-water pressure can also reduce effective stress and frictional resistance along a potential slip surface. Drainage, cohesion, slope geometry and material properties influence stability, so the effect is not explained by added mass alone.

misconceptions.claim: Rain can destabilise a slope only by making the material heavier.
misconceptions.truth: Added water can increase weight, but rising pore-water pressure can also reduce effective stress and frictional resistance along a potential slip surface. Drainage, cohesion, slope geometry and material properties influence stability, so the effect is not explained by added mass alone.

teacher.script:
Locate crown, curved shear surface and toe. Read the assumed strength and initial factor of safety.

Increase Pore pressure and relate falling resistance to effective stress. At the highest setting, play the prescribed rotational movement.
pitfalls: Consider slope material, gravity and water pressure together rather than attributing every failure to wave erosion.
Distinguish a rockfall from a slide or flow by describing how the material moves.
Explain how saturation can reduce slope stability, including on slopes that are not beside the sea.

modelNotes: A simplified Bishop calculation divides the initial sliding mass into 160 vertical slices.
Effective cohesion is 2 kPa, friction angle 15°, and soil unit weight 20 kN/m³.

labs.title: Rain shadow
labs.hook: Rising air expands and cools.
labs.objective: Explain why rising air cools and produces rain on a windward slope, leaving drier conditions on the leeward side.

steps.title: Observe
steps.body: Predict which side rises and cools. Set Initial humidity to 20% and Ridge height to 900 m: no cloud forms.

steps.title: Tinker
steps.body: Compare 70% and 2100 m; follow the parcel through cloud base. Read temperatures at both feet and explain the difference.

steps.title: Explain
steps.body: Why can air arrive at the leeward foot of a mountain warmer and drier than when it began rising?

steps.title: Check
steps.body: Choose an answer and explain your reasoning. Each question includes feedback.

questions.prompt: Air rising on the windward slope…
questions.explain: Rising air encounters lower pressure, expands and cools. If it cools to saturation, water vapour can condense into cloud droplets.

choices: Leeward of a barrier, where air has already dropped its water
questions.explain: Air crossing a mountain can lose moisture on the windward side and then warm as it descends downwind. The resulting lower relative humidity helps create a drier leeward region.

questions.prompt: If this model ridge rises above the parcel condensation level…
choices: Condensation and a warmer, drier leeward arrival can develop.
questions.explain: Once the parcel rises above its condensation level, latent heat release reduces its cooling rate during further ascent. Subsequent descent can bring it to the same elevation warmer and less humid, although this model does not calculate rainfall totals.

questions.prompt: Owens Valley east of the Sierra is dry for the same reason Penrith is drier than Keswick because…
choices: Both sit in a transform fault
Moist air rose, rained, and descended dry
questions.explain: Both examples involve moist air rising over a barrier and descending on its sheltered side. Their rainfall contrasts also depend on prevailing winds, moisture supply and the wider regional climate.

why: Rising air expands and cools. If it reaches saturation, condensation can occur; after moisture is lost, descent on the far side of a ridge can bring warmer, drier air to the same elevation.
Compare 70% and 2100 m; follow the parcel through cloud base. Read temperatures at both feet and explain the difference.
The parcel uses simplified lapse rates and assumed condensate loss; it calculates a temperature comparison rather than rainfall amounts.

glossary.def: Precipitation associated with air being lifted over high ground. Rising air expands and cools; if it becomes saturated, cloud can form and precipitation may follow. The lee side may receive less rain, depending on the wider weather pattern.

A relatively dry area on the sheltered side of high ground. Uplift and precipitation can remove moisture from approaching air, while descending air warms and its relative humidity falls. Prevailing winds influence the strength of the effect.

The side of a feature that faces the approaching wind. Moist air forced upward there may form cloud and rain. Windward is relative to wind direction, so it does not always mean the same compass-facing slope.
The side sheltered from the prevailing wind. Descending air there often warms and has lower relative humidity.
Cooling as an air parcel expands when pressure falls, without exchanging heat with its surroundings. Rising air commonly cools this way.

A warm, often dry wind descending on the sheltered side of a mountain range. Air warms as it is compressed during descent, and moisture loss or differences in source air can intensify the effect. Föhn and chinook are regional names.
In a rain-shadow model, high ground that forces approaching air to rise; its height and orientation influence uplift.

misconception.claim: A mountain creates the moisture that falls as rain on its windward side.
misconception.truth: The approaching air already contains water vapour. Forced uplift makes the air expand and cool; if saturation is reached, condensation and precipitation may follow. After moisture loss, descending air can become warmer and drier on the leeward side, although the outcome depends on the incoming conditions.

misconceptions.claim: A mountain creates the moisture that falls as rain on its windward side.
misconceptions.truth: The approaching air already contains water vapour. Forced uplift makes the air expand and cool; if saturation is reached, condensation and precipitation may follow. After moisture loss, descending air can become warmer and drier on the leeward side, although the outcome depends on the incoming conditions.

teacher.script:
Predict which side rises and cools. Set Initial humidity to 20% and Ridge height to 900 m: no cloud forms.

Compare 70% and 2100 m; follow the parcel through cloud base. Read temperatures at both feet and explain the difference.
pitfalls: Explain that uplift can cool moist air to condensation; a mountain does not create the water vapour.
Distinguish local windward and leeward contrasts from broad climate patterns associated with latitude.
Use long-term climate evidence before classifying a relatively dry valley as a desert.

modelNotes: Unsaturated ascent is approximately 9.8 °C per kilometre.
Above it, the calculation uses a fixed saturated lapse rate of 6 °C/km; real values vary with temperature and pressure.
Vertical relief is enlarged 2.5 times; Physical scale restores a common distance scale.

labs.title: Groundwater
labs.hook: Groundwater fills connected pores and fractures below the water table.
labs.objective: Locate water in connected pores and explain how pumping changes the water table and flow towards a well.

steps.title: Observe
steps.body: Name the saturated pores and water table before pumping. Raise Pump and compare the well head with the fixed boundary.

steps.title: Tinker
steps.body: Switch to Confined aquifer: the gold surface is pressure head, not a lake.

steps.title: Explain
steps.body: How does lowering the water level in a well change the hydraulic gradient around it?

steps.title: Check
steps.body: Choose an answer and explain your reasoning. Each question includes feedback.

choices: An underground lake with a shore
The top of the saturated zone in the pores
A river under the ground always
questions.explain: The water table is the upper surface of the saturated zone in an unconfined aquifer. Beneath it, connected pores and fractures are filled with water rather than air.

choices: A rock or sediment that stores and yields useful water
questions.explain: An aquifer must both store groundwater and transmit it readily enough to supply useful quantities. High water content alone is insufficient if pore connections or fractures do not allow water to flow.

questions.prompt: In this steady unconfined model, increasing pumping makes the nearby water table…
choices: Lower into a cone of depression.
questions.explain: Pumping lowers hydraulic head near the well, creating a gradient that draws groundwater towards it. This steady model balances that inflow against pumping and does not track long-term exhaustion of a finite store.

questions.prompt: Yorkshire Chalk and the Ogallala are paired in this lab because…
choices: Both are major aquifers people actually drink, one UK, one US
questions.explain: Both the Chalk and Ogallala aquifers store and supply groundwater, but water moves through different geological structures. The comparison helps separate the shared storage-and-flow principles from differences in rock properties.

why: Groundwater fills connected pores and fractures below the water table. Pumping lowers hydraulic head near a well, creating a gradient that draws water towards it.
Switch to Confined aquifer: the gold surface is pressure head, not a lake.
The steady-flow calculation holds the outer head fixed; it does not determine recharge, long-term depletion or sustainable abstraction.

glossary.def: The upper surface of an unconfined groundwater body, below which connected pores are saturated. Its height changes with recharge and groundwater flow. In a confined aquifer, the level reached in a well represents pressure head rather than a free water table.

A body of permeable rock or sediment that stores groundwater and allows useful amounts to flow through it. Water occupies connected pores or fractures; an aquifer is usually not an underground lake. Both storage space and connectivity matter.
A layer of rock or sediment with low permeability that slows groundwater flow. It may confine an aquifer without being completely impermeable.

A lowering of the water table or groundwater pressure surface around a pumping well. Water flows towards the well down this hydraulic gradient. The cone is a pattern in water levels, not an empty cone excavated in the rock.

The addition of water to an aquifer, usually as infiltrated rainfall or surface water percolates downwards. Recharge may take time and vary strongly by season and geology. It is not identical to all rainfall falling on the land above.

A line of springs where groundwater emerges along a geological or topographic boundary, often where permeable rock meets less permeable material. Its position reflects underground flow paths and can help explain the location of settlements.
A saturated permeable layer bounded above by a low-permeability layer. Water in a well rises to its pressure level, which may or may not reach the ground surface.

misconception.claim: Groundwater usually occupies a single underground lake.
misconception.truth: Most groundwater occupies connected pores and fractures in rock or sediment. In an unconfined aquifer, the water table marks the top of the saturated zone. In a confined aquifer, water in a well may rise above the aquifer because of pressure rather than an underground open lake.
