misconceptions.claim: Groundwater usually occupies a single underground lake.
misconceptions.truth: Most groundwater occupies connected pores and fractures in rock or sediment. In an unconfined aquifer, the water table marks the top of the saturated zone. In a confined aquifer, water in a well may rise above the aquifer because of pressure rather than an underground open lake.

teacher.script:
Name the saturated pores and water table before pumping. Raise Pump and compare the well head with the fixed boundary.

Switch to Confined aquifer: the gold surface is pressure head, not a lake.
pitfalls: Show groundwater occupying pores and fractures rather than presenting underground rivers as the usual arrangement.
Explain that pumping removes water from an existing store and can lower the water table.
Distinguish a rock’s ability to store water from its ability to transmit enough water to act as a useful aquifer.

modelNotes: Hydraulic conductivity is 10 m/day, well radius 0.2 m, outer radius 500 m and confined thickness 12 m.

labs.title: Isostasy
labs.hook: Adding an ice load changes the equilibrium height of the crust.
labs.objective: Explain how the crust responds to loading and unloading, using an ice sheet to explore subsidence and rebound.

steps.title: Observe
steps.body: Identify crust, root and solid mantle. Set the ice load to zero, then 3000 m. Predict the direction of motion.

steps.title: Tinker
steps.body: Calculate 3000 × 917/3300 and compare the displayed depression. Switch to physical scale to see the vertical and horizontal dimensions at the same scale.

steps.title: Explain
steps.body: Explain why adding an ice load depresses the crust and why removing it allows rebound.

steps.title: Check
steps.body: Choose an answer and explain your reasoning. Each question includes feedback.

choices: The crust floats in a denser mantle, like wood in water
questions.explain: Isostasy describes the tendency towards gravitational balance between lithospheric loads and the material beneath them. The mantle is mostly solid but can deform and flow over geological timescales.

questions.prompt: After an ice sheet melts, the land…
choices: Rises as the mantle flows back — glacial rebound
questions.explain: Removing an ice sheet reduces the load on the lithosphere, allowing uplift as the underlying mantle readjusts. This response can continue for thousands of years after the ice has melted.

questions.prompt: If I add ice on the slider, the crustal block should…
questions.explain: Adding ice increases the weight supported by the underlying material. In this local balance model, the crustal block sinks farther to displace enough denser mantle to support the added load.

questions.prompt: What process links raised beaches in western Scotland with the rising shore of Hudson Bay?
choices: Both unloaded ice and the crust is still rebounding
questions.explain: Both regions carried thick ice sheets whose removal initiated ongoing crustal uplift. Raised shorelines record the resulting change in land level relative to the sea, together with any sea-level changes.

why: Adding an ice load changes the equilibrium height of the crust. In the local Airy model, a denser mantle supports a less dense crustal column, and unloading raises its equilibrium position.
Calculate 3000 × 917/3300 and compare the displayed depression. Switch to physical scale to see the vertical and horizontal dimensions at the same scale.
The experiment calculates an equilibrium displacement; actual rebound takes time as the solid mantle deforms.

glossary.def: The gravitational balance in which the lithosphere is supported by denser material beneath it. Adding or removing a large load causes deformation and adjustment over time. The mantle flows slowly as solid rock rather than as a simple liquid ocean.

The gradual rise of land following the removal of a large ice load. The solid Earth adjusts as mantle material flows slowly over time. Rebound changes relative sea level locally, even while global mean sea level may rise.
A former beach now above present sea level because of land uplift, a fall in sea level, or both.

Earth’s rigid outer mechanical layer, comprising the crust and the uppermost mantle. It is divided into tectonic plates and overlies the weaker asthenosphere. The lithosphere is therefore thicker than the crust alone.
A mechanically weak part of the upper mantle beneath the lithosphere. It is predominantly solid rock that deforms slowly over geological time.

In isostasy, the thickened lower part of continental crust beneath a mountain belt. Less dense crust extends deeper into the mantle and helps support high topography. The term describes crustal structure, not a literal plant-like shape.
Describing a change in global mean sea level, for example from changing ocean-water volume or ocean-basin capacity.

misconception.claim: Postglacial rebound shows that the mantle beneath the crust is liquid lava.
misconception.truth: The mantle is predominantly solid rock but can deform slowly over long timescales. Removing an ice load changes the equilibrium supported by the underlying material, allowing the land to rise over time. An equilibrium-height model does not by itself calculate how fast that rebound occurs.

misconceptions.claim: Postglacial rebound shows that the mantle beneath the crust is liquid lava.
misconceptions.truth: The mantle is predominantly solid rock but can deform slowly over long timescales. Removing an ice load changes the equilibrium supported by the underlying material, allowing the land to rise over time. An equilibrium-height model does not by itself calculate how fast that rebound occurs.

teacher.script:
Identify crust, root and solid mantle. Set the ice load to zero, then 3000 m. Predict the direction of motion.

Calculate 3000 × 917/3300 and compare the displayed depression. Switch to physical scale to see the vertical and horizontal dimensions at the same scale.
pitfalls: Explain how the lithosphere responds to loading rather than treating the crust as resting on a rigid floor.
Describe the mantle as predominantly solid material that can flow slowly over long timescales.
Distinguish local changes in relative sea level caused by rebound from changes in global sea level.

modelNotes: This local Airy experiment keeps a 35 km crustal column unchanged and adds up to 3000 m of ice.
Crust, mantle and ice densities are 2800, 3300 and 917 kg/m³.
Equal mass above a compensation depth gives an equilibrium depression of ice thickness × 917/3300.

labs.title: Wilson cycle
labs.hook: Continental rifting can open an ocean basin, while subduction can later consume oceanic lithosphere and bring continents together.
labs.objective: Follow the opening and closing of an ocean basin and relate continental collision to the formation of mountain belts.

steps.title: Observe
steps.body: Choose Continental rift, then Young ocean. Locate the ridge and thin oceanic crust in Open ocean.

steps.title: Tinker
steps.body: Switch to Subduction begins and follow the slab. Compare Ocean closes with Continental collision and identify the root.

steps.title: Explain
steps.body: How does subduction turn an expanding ocean into a closing basin?

steps.title: Check
steps.body: Choose an answer and explain your reasoning. Each question includes feedback.

choices: Oceans opening and closing over geologic time
questions.explain: Continental rifting can open an ocean basin, while later subduction can consume its oceanic lithosphere and bring continents together again. The Wilson cycle summarises these possible stages over geological time.

choices: An older ocean that opened and then collided shut
questions.explain: Parts of the Caledonian and Appalachian mountain belts preserve evidence of convergence and collisions associated with closure of the Iapetus Ocean. Later Atlantic opening separated sections of that older mountain system.

questions.prompt: If I scrub the stage slider toward collision, the ocean should…
questions.explain: As subduction consumes oceanic lithosphere, the basin narrows and the bordering continents approach one another. Continental collision then shortens and thickens crust, producing a mountain belt.

questions.prompt: Iceland on today’s Mid-Atlantic is which stage?
questions.explain: Iceland lies on the active Mid-Atlantic spreading ridge, where plates separate and new oceanic crust forms. It therefore represents ongoing ocean-basin opening rather than closure by continental collision.

why: Continental rifting can open an ocean basin, while subduction can later consume oceanic lithosphere and bring continents together. Mountain belts can preserve evidence of oceans that have closed.
Switch to Subduction begins and follow the slab. Compare Ocean closes with Continental collision and identify the root.
The six stages organise possible tectonic changes; they are not a fixed schedule followed by every ocean basin.

glossary.def: A framework describing the opening and eventual closing of an ocean basin through rifting, seafloor spreading, subduction and continental collision. Different basins follow different histories. Geological structures can preserve evidence of stages even after an ocean has disappeared.
An elongated region where the lithosphere is extending and thinning. Some continental rifts develop into ocean basins; others cease spreading.

A transition between continental and oceanic crust that is not an active plate boundary. Many Atlantic margins developed after continental rifting. Sediment accumulation, subsidence and occasional earthquakes can still occur, so passive does not mean completely inactive.

A period or process of mountain building involving deformation and thickening of the crust. Plate collision and subduction are common settings. Mountains may later be eroded, leaving folded rocks and other evidence of an older mountain belt.
An ancient mountain belt formed during Palaeozoic continental collisions, now exposed in places including Scotland, Scandinavia and Greenland.
An ancient mountain belt in eastern North America, assembled through several Palaeozoic collisions during the closing of oceans and formation of Pangaea.
A body of crust with a geological history distinct from neighbouring regions, often joined to a continent by tectonic accretion.

misconception.claim: Every ocean basin follows the same fixed timetable from opening to closure.
misconception.truth: The Wilson cycle organises possible stages of rifting, ocean spreading, subduction and collision. Real basins differ in geometry, plate motions and duration, and some rifts stop developing. The framework helps interpret geological evidence without prescribing one schedule for every ocean.

misconceptions.claim: Every ocean basin follows the same fixed timetable from opening to closure.
misconceptions.truth: The Wilson cycle organises possible stages of rifting, ocean spreading, subduction and collision. Real basins differ in geometry, plate motions and duration, and some rifts stop developing. The framework helps interpret geological evidence without prescribing one schedule for every ocean.

cases.label: A different job on a different edge

teacher.script:
Choose Continental rift, then Young ocean. Locate the ridge and thin oceanic crust in Open ocean.

Switch to Subduction begins and follow the slab. Compare Ocean closes with Continental collision and identify the root.
pitfalls: Use Pangaea as one example within a longer history of continental assembly and breakup.
Place Iceland at a divergent boundary rather than using it as an example of continental collision.
Connect the closing of an ocean with later mountain building while allowing for more complex histories in real regions.

modelNotes: The unstretched reference continent is 35 km thick and the oceanic crust about 7 km thick; both overlie solid mantle.
Physical scale restores a common scale in this ideal 300 km cross-section, which is only part of a basin.

labs.title: Soil catena
labs.hook: Soils along a slope are linked by movement of water and sediment.
labs.objective: Compare soil profiles from the crest to the foot of a slope and explain how water and sediment movement connect them.

steps.title: Observe
steps.body: Locate crest, backslope and toe on one parent material. Read the three soil thicknesses.

steps.title: Tinker
steps.body: Increase Slope and compare export and accumulation in this selected example. Compare physical scale and distinguish soil thickness from topographic relief.

steps.title: Explain
steps.body: How can movement of water and sediment connect soil differences along a single slope?

steps.title: Check
steps.body: Choose an answer and explain your reasoning. Each question includes feedback.

choices: A sequence of soils down one slope, linked by water and sediment
questions.explain: A catena links soils along a slope where drainage and the transfer of material vary with topographic position. These differences can produce distinct profiles even where the parent material is similar.

questions.prompt: Why may an upper-slope soil be thinner than the toe soil?
choices: Water and sediment can leave the upper slope and accumulate downslope.
It sits on an aquifer lake
questions.explain: Erosion can remove material from upper slopes while deposition adds it near the foot of a slope. The resulting thickness pattern also depends on soil formation, drainage and local conditions.

questions.prompt: Steepening the slope in this prescribed example makes the backslope soil…
choices: Thinner according to the selected comparison relationship.
questions.explain: This comparison assigns a thinner backslope soil as the selected slope increases. It illustrates a possible relationship but does not calculate a measured erosion rate from gradient alone.

questions.prompt: A Yorkshire valley side and an Iowa loess hill pair because…
choices: Both show crest-to-toe change on one material
questions.explain: Both examples compare soils at different positions along a slope rather than assuming a whole region has one profile. Keeping parent material similar helps reveal the effects of drainage and downslope transport.

why: Soils along a slope are linked by movement of water and sediment. Upper slopes may lose material while lower slopes receive it, creating differences even where parent material is similar.
Increase Slope and compare export and accumulation in this selected example. Compare physical scale and distinguish soil thickness from topographic relief.
The selected thickness pattern is one example; climate, drainage and land use can produce a different catena.

glossary.def: A sequence of soils along a slope whose differences are related to relief, drainage and movement of sediment. Compare a freely drained crest with a wetter footslope. A catena need not form a perfectly regular sequence in every landscape.
The highest part of a hill or ridge. Soil thickness and drainage there depend on the local relief, geology and climate.
The main, usually steep section of a hillslope between its shoulder and footslope; material commonly moves through it downslope.
The downslope end of a landslide or other mass-movement deposit. Displaced material may thicken or bulge there as it slows. It differs from the crown, where material separates from the stable slope.
Soil features associated with prolonged saturation and oxygen shortage, often including grey colours and rusty mottles from changes in iron chemistry.
A traditional soil term for a shallow, often acidic soil over hard, non-calcareous rock; commonly found on steep or exposed ground.

Loose sediment accumulated on or near the foot of a slope through gravity-driven movement and surface wash. It commonly contains a mixture of particle sizes. Unlike alluvium, it is not defined by deposition from a river channel.

misconception.claim: Soils on one hillside must be identical because they share a climate.
misconception.truth: Position on a slope affects drainage, erosion, deposition and the movement of dissolved material. These differences can produce contrasting soils even on similar parent material under the same regional climate. The pattern depends on local conditions rather than a universal sequence of thicknesses.

misconceptions.claim: Soils on one hillside must be identical because they share a climate.
misconceptions.truth: Position on a slope affects drainage, erosion, deposition and the movement of dissolved material. These differences can produce contrasting soils even on similar parent material under the same regional climate. The pattern depends on local conditions rather than a universal sequence of thicknesses.

teacher.script:
Locate crest, backslope and toe on one parent material. Read the three soil thicknesses.

Increase Slope and compare export and accumulation in this selected example. Compare physical scale and distinguish soil thickness from topographic relief.
pitfalls: Consider slope position, drainage and material movement alongside climate when comparing soils along a hillslope.
Use evidence of erosion and accumulation rather than assuming that the thickest soil must occur at the crest.
Distinguish a catena’s sequence of soil profiles from a texture triangle that classifies mineral particle proportions.

modelNotes: This illustrative 120 m hillslope has crest, backslope and toe stations.

labs.title: Periglacial landforms
labs.hook: Permafrost is ground that remains at or below 0 °C for at least two years.
labs.objective: Explain how repeated freezing and thawing produce ice wedges and patterned ground in cold landscapes.

steps.title: Observe
steps.body: Define permafrost and distinguish ground ice from a glacier. Play a year and identify seasonal thaw above the dashed maximum active-layer depth.

steps.title: Tinker
steps.body: Increase Wedge development and trace the tapering ice mass. Explain winter thermal contraction, crack infilling and refreezing.

steps.title: Explain
steps.body: Explain how repeated thermal cracking and refreezing build an ice wedge over many years.

steps.title: Check
steps.body: Choose an answer and explain your reasoning. Each question includes feedback.

choices: Cold-climate processes at the edge of, or without, glacier ice
questions.explain: Periglacial environments are dominated by cold-ground processes such as seasonal freezing and, in some settings, permafrost. They do not require a glacier to occupy the site.

choices: Winter cracks fill with water or snow, freeze, and widen the crack year on year
questions.explain: Strong winter cooling can crack frozen ground, and meltwater entering the cracks can freeze. Repeated cracking and ice addition over many years can build a wedge of ground ice.

questions.prompt: What does Wedge development change here?
choices: The date of the next glacier.
A prescribed ice-wedge width, without assigning years or a rate.
questions.explain: Wedge development changes a prescribed geometry so that different accumulated widths can be compared. The seasonal animation is separate and does not assign an observed growth rate to that change.

questions.prompt: Cairngorm blockfields and Alaskan ice-wedge polygons pair because…
choices: Both are freeze–thaw factories without needing a valley glacier on the spot
questions.explain: Blockfields and ice-wedge polygons illustrate different processes associated with cold ground. Neither requires the local landscape to have been carved by an actively flowing valley glacier.

why: Permafrost is ground that remains at or below 0 °C for at least two years. Seasonal thaw affects its active layer, while repeated thermal cracking and refreezing can build ice wedges.
Increase Wedge development and trace the tapering ice mass. Explain winter thermal contraction, crack infilling and refreezing.
The annual cycle and accumulated wedge width are separate comparisons; the width slider does not specify a growth rate.

glossary.def: Describing processes and landforms associated with cold ground, including freeze–thaw, frost sorting and thermal cracking. They may occur near glaciers or far from present ice. Relict features can remain after a region’s climate has become warmer.
A wedge of ground ice formed as water enters thermal-contraction cracks and freezes repeatedly in permafrost.
Repeated ground patterns such as polygons, circles or stripes, produced by processes including frost sorting and thermal contraction in cold environments.
Weathering, meltwater movement and other processes around persistent snow patches that can help enlarge shallow hollows.

An extensive cover of angular rock blocks, often found on cold upland plateaus. Frost action can contribute to its development, but the blocks may record a long history of weathering. Their presence alone does not prove that permafrost exists today.

The ground above permafrost that thaws in summer and freezes again in winter. Its thickness changes with local climate, vegetation and soil. Seasonal thaw of this layer does not necessarily mean that the underlying permafrost has disappeared.
Ground that remains at or below 0 °C for at least two consecutive years. It may contain ice but need not be permanently ice-filled.

Seasonal thaw can affect the active layer above it, while glaciers are separate bodies of accumulated, flowing ice.

labs.title: Storm surge
labs.hook: Onshore winds push water towards the coast, while lower atmospheric pressure also raises the water surface.
labs.objective: Explain how strong winds and low atmospheric pressure can raise coastal water levels, especially over a shallow shelf.

steps.title: Observe
steps.body: Set wind and pressure drop to zero and identify the reference sea level. Raise Onshore wind and compare two shelf depths.

steps.title: Tinker
steps.body: Set wind to zero and isolate a pressure drop of 3000 Pa. Combine the effects, then compare physical scale to discuss geometric scale.

steps.title: Explain
steps.body: Why can the same onshore wind produce a larger rise in water level over a shallower shelf?

steps.title: Check
steps.body: Choose an answer and explain your reasoning. Each question includes feedback.

choices: Wind-driven pile-up of water on a shallow shelf, plus low pressure
questions.explain: Onshore winds can push seawater towards a coast, and low atmospheric pressure can also raise sea level. Shallow shelves and coastal geometry can amplify the resulting storm surge.

choices: A sudden shift of the water column, often seafloor slip
questions.explain: Rapid displacement of a large volume of water generates a tsunami, often following vertical seafloor motion. Storm surge instead develops through atmospheric forcing by winds and pressure.

questions.prompt: If I raise the wind slider toward the coast, the water should…
questions.explain: Stronger onshore wind applies greater stress to the water surface and drives more water towards the coast. In the model, the resulting setup also depends on shelf depth.

questions.prompt: 1953 eastern England and Katrina’s Gulf Coast pair because…
choices: Both were wind and pressure piling water onto a shallow coast
questions.explain: Both events involved storm winds and low pressure raising coastal water levels over shallow margins. Their different storm types and coastlines affected the timing, extent and severity of the flooding.

glossary.def: A rise in sea level above the expected tide, driven mainly by storm winds and atmospheric pressure. Coastal shape and water depth influence its size. Surge combines with tides and waves to determine coastal water levels and flooding.

A rise in water level where persistent wind pushes water towards a shore. It contributes to storm surge, particularly over shallow shelves and within bays. Its size depends on wind, duration, depth and coastal shape.

The tendency for sea level to rise where atmospheric pressure falls, and fall where pressure rises. A rough equilibrium estimate is about 1 cm per hectopascal. Storm surge also depends strongly on winds and coastal geometry.

The shallow, gently sloping submerged edge of a continent, extending towards a steeper continental slope. Shelf depth and shape influence tides, waves and storm surge. A shallow shelf can support greater wind-driven water-level rise for the same forcing.

A series of long waves generated by rapid displacement of water, most commonly during a large undersea earthquake. In shallow water they slow and can grow in height. Tsunamis are not caused by the normal daily tides.
Flooding described by the water level after short-period surface waves are averaged out. Coastal still-water level can include the tide and storm surge.
An elongated sandy island lying roughly parallel to the coast, separated from the mainland by a lagoon or other shallow water.

misconception.claim: A hurricane’s wind category fully describes its coastal flood threat.
misconception.truth: Coastal water rise also depends on storm size, track, duration, atmospheric pressure and the shape and depth of the coast. Tide, waves and river flow further affect flooding. A wind category therefore cannot specify the water level or inundation at a particular location.
